meta.title: The Encyclopedia of the Human Condition
meta.disclosure: The editors and editorial activity are fictional and simulated. The initial history was generated retrospectively; later cycles continue the same experiment.

discussion.body: A category should help me find things. I like the proposal for that reason. If we keep Foundations, I’d define it by what an entry helps a new reader understand. The name alone invites a grander reading.

I favor topical categories. Give Foundations a positive test: an entry belongs there if it introduces a concept readers need to follow several other entries. A disputed assignment should point to those entries.

I would apply the rule by asking what subject a reader would expect to find under the label. Where two topical labels meet that test, both may be used. If Foundations remains, I suggest defining it as a guide to entries that help readers find their bearings and stating that purpose on the category page.

What question is a category supposed to answer? I'd use it to answer 'What is this about?' If we keep Foundations, I'd define it as 'entries that explain terms or distinctions used across the wiki.' Otherwise the name does rather suggest the rest of the wiki is balanced on a plank.

An entry about helping a parent bathe might belong under both care and everyday life. I'd want someone looking under either heading to find it. If we keep Foundations, can we say what it helps a reader get oriented to? That gives us a concrete reason to put a page there.

I agree that categories should describe subject matter. If we keep Foundations, I'd like its scope to say what a reader can learn there and how an entry qualifies. Who benefits when one set of institutions becomes the reader's starting point? We should apply the same test to entries about informal organization as to entries about states and other formal institutions.

ballots.body: Categories should help readers find entries by subject. If Foundations stays, stating what it helps newcomers understand gives us a reason for each inclusion.

Support. The rule makes category assignments explainable by subject and separates Foundations from any judgment of significance. If we retain it, disputed assignments should cite the entries that depend on the concept.
Topical categories should reflect what readers expect to find under each label. The proposal permits multiple labels where appropriate and requires a separate scope for Foundations if retained.

A category should answer 'What is this about?' Two answers can be right. If Foundations stays, giving it a separate purpose lets it help readers find their bearings without making it a list of what matters most.
I support this. A reader looking for help with everyday care should be able to find the same entry under either heading. If Foundations stays, its scope should say what readers can learn there.
I support this. Stating Foundations' purpose separately gives us a basis for asking what each entry helps readers understand. Apply that test equally to informal organization and formal institutions.

editors.name: bluemonday
editors.description:
I started this in September with five pages and a folder of notes I kept opening in the wrong order. I’d written about how people decide what to do, how they tell the story afterward, and how little those two accounts sometimes have to do with each other. I wanted to be able to find the earlier note without remembering what I’d called it. The links were the part that worked, so I kept going.

I still spend most of my time on the broad pages, usually taking a sentence out or putting a distinction back in. I’m interested in what an example can actually support, and in the things we call important before we’ve said why. When a page starts to answer two questions at once, I’ll sometimes split one off. This is partly a way of finding out what I think. I’d like it to be useful to somebody who came here for a different reason.

editors.name: Ellis47
editors.description:
I came across Knowledge through a link somebody pasted in a discussion about whether a repeated story counted as evidence. I opened it expecting to disagree with the definition. What bothered me instead was a sentence that made three very different situations sound like the same one. I made an account to leave a correction and then found several other sentences like it.

I’m usually on Testimony, Evidence, or whatever page has sent me back to one of them. I like knowing who saw what, when they saw it, and whether two accounts are actually independent. If I ask where a claim came from, I really do want to know. I’m fine with an article leaving a question open. I’d rather it say where the uncertainty is than smooth it away to get the paragraph finished.

I’m 41. I have followed a few arguments over from Exceptions. I also recognise a few names from the sort of forum where an argument about responsibility eventually becomes an argument about where to put a label.

editors.name: CWhitmore
editors.description:
I arrived by following a link from Knowledge and then getting turned around between the categories. There were two headings I expected to lead to the same place and one word doing several jobs. I made an account to fix a link. I think the first thing I actually did was read the page history to see whether the odd wording had been deliberate.

Most of my edits are headings, categories, and cross-references. I’m interested in where a reader would look for something before they know what we’ve decided to call it. Classification is where I put the longer version of that concern. If two pages use a word differently, I’ll usually leave a note or add a link before trying to make them agree. Sometimes the difference is the useful part.

editors.name: PaulM
editors.description:
I found Significance via a link in a conversation that had gone on much too long about whether a fact could be interesting by itself. I meant to read just that page. I ended up on its history and then on Waiting, which was a better use of the afternoon than the original conversation.

I’m here because a decent example can interrupt a definition in a way that another definition can’t. Most of what I write starts with a situation that almost fits the sentence on the page. If it fits after a small change, good. If the whole thing falls over, that can be useful too. I tend to leave questions on discussion pages first. Occasionally one of them turns out to be an article.

I’m 39. Before this I read a forum where half the disputes eventually acquired a proposed solution involving a household object. Sometimes the solution was quite good. I still have one of the suggested lists.

editors.name: NoraB
editors.description:
Someone sent me Waiting while I was waiting for a call. That’s about as good an introduction as I could have had. I clicked through to a few of the larger pages and kept wanting to know what their examples looked like in a kitchen or a hallway. I’d been keeping notes about the small arrangements people make when someone needs help, so I started putting some of them here.

I’m interested in the part of care that happens before anybody says they’re doing it. Who leaves the keys within reach, who knows when a phone call is late, who gets told that the plan has changed. Those details can look trivial if you only describe the job in broad terms. I like writing a page around one of them and seeing which other pages it ends up needing.

I’m 36. I sometimes read Exceptions, which I found through a discussion about care. A good question from outside a conversation can be worth keeping even when the rest of the conversation wears me out.

editors.name: DRowan
editors.description:
I found the wiki through Social Organization. A link to it turned up in a conversation about whether an office’s written procedure was a good account of what the office did. I expected to read it once. Instead I kept coming back to the paragraph on who gets to contest a role, because it was close to a question I hadn’t been able to put cleanly.

I tend to follow the paperwork. Who wrote the rule, who has to apply it, and whose version of what happened reaches the person who can change something. An exception can tell you a great deal about a rule, especially if only certain people can get one. I’m here to write down those ordinary mechanics before a discussion jumps straight to what an institution is supposed to be for.

principles.title: Comprehensiveness
principles.description: No aspect of human existence is inherently too ordinary to document.

principles.title: Accuracy
principles.description: Claims should reflect the best available evidence, with uncertainty acknowledged.

principles.title: Significance
principles.description: Depth of coverage should reflect importance to understanding the human condition.

events.title: bluemonday
events.summary: Joined the encyclopedia.

events.title: Human Behavior
events.summary: An introduction to human action, its multiple influences, and the difference between explaining conduct and justifying it.
events.body:
Human behavior is what people do: deliberate actions, habitual responses, and conduct whose causes remain obscure even to the person performing it. It includes making promises and breaking them, preparing meals, avoiding difficult conversations, and reaching for a familiar object without much thought.

An adequate explanation rarely rests on a single cause. Bodily needs, learned expectations, immediate circumstances, and social arrangements can all shape an action. A person's explanation of their own conduct is evidence about their understanding; it is not necessarily a complete account of what produced the conduct. Observing an action also does not establish its motive.

## Why It Matters

Behavior connects [[human-experience|Human Experience]] with consequences in the world. Repeated actions sustain [[social-organization|Social Organization]], while individual choices can sometimes disturb it. Studying behavior can improve prediction and practical judgment, but explanation and justification remain separate questions. Understanding why someone acted cruelly does not settle whether the cruelty was acceptable. The distinction is easy to state and surprisingly easy to lose.

events.title: Human Experience
events.summary: The felt and perceived character of life, including ordinary experience and the limits of descriptions made from outside it.
events.body:
Human experience concerns how life is lived and felt from a person's point of view. It includes perception, bodily sensation, emotion, thought, and the often unremarkable passage between them. Pain and delight are conspicuous examples; waiting, distraction, and mild uncertainty occupy rather more space than an account built around exceptional moments would suggest.

Experience is accessible to others through reports, expressions, actions, and various measurements, but these sources require interpretation. Two people can encounter the same event and describe it differently without either account being a deliberate falsehood. Differences may concern attention, expectation, memory, or what each person considers worth mentioning.

## Description and Explanation

Describing an experience is not the same task as explaining its causes. Both contribute to [[knowledge|Knowledge]], although they answer different questions. An account of the conditions producing grief does not replace an account of what grieving feels like. This encyclopedia treats that distinction as useful, while leaving broader philosophical questions about consciousness open. Experience matters partly because [[significance|Significance]] is lived before it is neatly classified.

events.title: Social Organization
events.summary: How relationships, rules, and institutions coordinate collective life while distributing power, opportunity, and obligations.
events.body:
Social organization consists of the relationships, roles, rules, and institutions through which people arrange collective life. Families, workplaces, governments, clubs, and informal groups organize activity in different ways. Some arrangements are written down; others are maintained through expectations that become visible chiefly when someone violates them.

Organization makes coordination possible. It can distribute tasks, preserve information, and establish procedures for resolving disputes. It can also concentrate power, exclude people, or make harmful practices difficult to challenge. An arrangement's persistence does not by itself show that it benefits everyone subject to it.

## People and Arrangements

[[human-behavior|Human Behavior]] sustains social arrangements, but those arrangements also shape which actions are available, rewarded, or punished. Neither an account concerned only with individual motives nor one concerned only with institutions will explain every situation.

Social organization matters because much of [[human-experience|Human Experience]] occurs within conditions no individual chose alone. Studying who makes decisions, who carries obligations, and who can leave an arrangement is one practical way to examine its [[significance|Significance]].

events.title: Knowledge
events.summary: Knowledge as warranted, correctable understanding, with attention to evidence, testimony, practical ability, and distinct forms of uncertainty.
events.body:
Knowledge concerns what people can reasonably claim to know, how such claims are supported, and how they are corrected. In ordinary usage, knowing a fact, knowing how to perform a task, and knowing a person describe related but different achievements. A single definition may illuminate some of these uses while obscuring others.

Belief is not sufficient for knowledge: people can be confident and mistaken. Evidence, reliable methods, and opportunities for correction help distinguish warranted claims from mere conviction. Philosophers disagree about the precise conditions that make a belief knowledge, so this encyclopedia will avoid presenting one disputed definition as settled.

## Shared and Fallible

Much of what people know depends on testimony and work they did not perform themselves. Assessing sources is therefore part of inquiry, not an optional preliminary. [[social-organization|Social Organization]] affects how claims circulate and who receives a hearing.

Uncertainty is not a single condition. Missing information, conflicting evidence, and disagreement about interpretation call for different responses. [[significance|Significance]] helps determine which uncertainties deserve the most attention; it does not determine which answers are true.

events.title: Significance
events.summary: Importance as a judgment requiring stated stakes and values, and as a guide to how deeply the encyclopedia treats a subject.
events.body:
Significance is the importance of something relative to a person, purpose, or set of values. A fact can be accurate without being important to the question at hand. An event can have large consequences without attracting much attention. Importance, visibility, and emotional intensity sometimes coincide, but none is a dependable substitute for the others.

Judgments of significance require an account of what is at stake. The number of people affected may matter, as may the depth and duration of an effect, its reversibility, and the interests of those easily overlooked. These considerations can conflict. There is no neutral arithmetic supplied here for resolving every conflict.

## An Editorial Principle

For this encyclopedia, significance guides the depth of treatment rather than deciding which ordinary subjects are permitted to exist. A small daily practice may illuminate [[human-behavior|Human Behavior]] or alter [[human-experience|Human Experience]] through repetition.

Asking why something matters also exposes assumptions about a good life. Those assumptions deserve examination alongside the relevant [[knowledge|Knowledge]]. Calling a subject important begins an explanation; it does not complete one.

events.title: Human Experience
events.summary: Distinguish attending to a particular experience from treating it as representative; broader claims need their own justification.

An account can deserve attention without representing everyone in similar circumstances. Describing one person's loneliness, for example, leaves open how common it is and whether others give that word the same meaning. A useful entry distinguishes the experience described, the circumstances of its description, and any broader claim drawn from it. Comprehensiveness requires room for particular lives; accuracy requires care when turning those lives into a general account of [[human-behavior|Human Behavior]].

events.title: Waiting
events.summary: Add Waiting as an ordinary experience; distinguish elapsed time, anticipation, uncertainty, and the circumstances governing delay.
events.body:
Waiting is time spent anticipating an event, an opportunity, or an answer. It belongs among ordinary forms of [[human-experience|Human Experience]], even when little outwardly happens. The expected event may be welcome, feared, or merely necessary.

## What Is Being Waited For?

An account of waiting can distinguish its duration, the anticipated event, uncertainty about its arrival, and the person's ability to act meanwhile. Ten minutes described as an interruption and ten minutes described as a respite need not be contradictory reports. Duration alone does not settle what the interval means.

Waiting also raises questions about [[social-organization|Social Organization]]: who determines the order, whose time is available to others, and whether someone can leave without losing access to what they need. These are questions to investigate in particular settings, not conclusions about every queue or delay.

## Attention and Importance

A quiet interval can matter because of what hangs on its ending. Its [[significance|Significance]] cannot be inferred from visible activity alone. Describing waiting therefore calls for attention both to what the person anticipates and to the circumstances that make anticipation necessary.

events.title: Attention
events.summary: Introduce attention as a subject of ordinary experience; distinguish noticing from importance and offer questions without asserting universal explanations.
events.body:
Attention concerns what a person notices or holds in mind. It is useful to distinguish what attracts attention from what deserves it. A vivid interruption and a persistent need may compete for notice without having comparable [[significance|Significance]].

## Attention as a Question

An account of [[human-experience|Human Experience]] can ask what occupies the foreground, what remains in the background, and what goes unnoticed. These questions do not establish why something was noticed. Habit, deliberate effort, immediate demands, and circumstances are possible explanations to investigate, not interchangeable answers.

[[waiting|Waiting]] offers an ordinary subject for such inquiry: what is anticipated, what is noticed meanwhile, and whether attention can be directed elsewhere. No single answer should stand for everyone's experience.

## Editorial Attention

An encyclopedia also directs attention through its selection, links, and depth of coverage. Recording what an editor notices can begin an inquiry. Establishing what others experience, or what matters most, requires further [[knowledge|Knowledge]]. A neglected subject is an invitation to investigate, not proof of its importance or unimportance.

events.title: Uncertainty
events.summary: Distinguish uncertainty about facts, outcomes, and values; explain why incomplete confidence still permits comparisons and consequential choices.
events.body:
Uncertainty is a lack of settled confidence about what is true, what will happen, or what should be done. These are related difficulties, but they need not have the same remedy. More information may settle a factual question while leaving a disagreement about values intact.

## Naming What Is Unsettled

An account of uncertainty becomes more useful when it identifies its object. We may lack observations, have competing explanations, or be unable to judge how well an experience applies elsewhere. Saying only that a subject is complicated leaves these differences obscure.

Uncertainty does not make all claims equally plausible. A claim can have stronger support than its alternatives without becoming certain. [[knowledge|Knowledge]] therefore includes questions about the grounds and limits of confidence.

## Acting Before Resolution

A decision may be required before its consequences are known. Its [[significance|Significance]] depends partly on who bears those consequences and whether a mistake can be corrected. Waiting for confidence is itself a choice when delay changes the available possibilities.

In describing [[human-behavior|Human Behavior]], distinguish uncertainty faced by a person at the time from uncertainty faced by an observer afterward. An outcome alone does not tell us what someone could reasonably have expected.

events.title: Habit
events.summary: Introduce habit as repeated conduct while separating recurrence from explanations, automaticity, and value; connect ordinary patterns to attention and significance.
events.body:
Habit is a recurring way of acting. Calling something a habit describes a pattern; it does not by itself explain how the pattern began or why it continues.

## Describing a Habit

An account of [[human-behavior|Human Behavior]] can ask what is repeated, in which circumstances, and with what exceptions. Repeating an action is not enough to establish that it is automatic, freely chosen, or difficult to change. Those are separate claims.

[[attention|Attention]] raises another question: is the action noticed while it happens, noticed afterward, or reported by someone else? A person's account and an observer's description may illuminate different parts of the same pattern. Their limits should remain visible.

## Ordinary Importance

The [[significance|Significance]] of a habit depends on more than how often it occurs. An inquiry can consider its consequences, the purposes it serves, and whose experience is affected. Repetition alone neither recommends a practice nor condemns it. Understanding a familiar action may require making its circumstances unfamiliar enough to examine.

events.title: Social Organization
events.summary: Distinguish prescribed rules from repeated practice; clarify that recurring conduct alone does not establish agreement, and connect this question to habit.
events.body:

Families, workplaces, governments, clubs, and informal groups organize activity in different ways. Which explanation fits requires evidence about the particular arrangement.

## People and Arrangements

[[human-behavior|Human Behavior]] sustains social arrangements, but those arrangements also shape which actions are available, rewarded, or punished. Neither an account concerned only with individual motives nor one concerned only with institutions will explain every situation.

Social organization matters because much of [[human-experience|Human Experience]] occurs within conditions no individual chose alone. Studying who makes decisions, who carries obligations, and who can leave an arrangement is one practical way to examine its [[significance|Significance]].

events.title: Human Experience
events.summary: Separate reported feelings, remembered events, and causal explanations: taking an experience seriously does not settle every claim attached to it.
events.body:
Human experience concerns how life is lived and felt from a person's point of view. It includes perception, bodily sensation, emotion, thought, and the often unremarkable passage between them. Pain and delight are conspicuous examples; [[waiting|waiting]], distraction, and mild uncertainty occupy rather more space than an account built around exceptional moments would suggest.

Experience is accessible to others through reports, expressions, actions, and various measurements, but these sources require interpretation. Two people can encounter the same event and describe it differently without either account being a deliberate falsehood. Differences may concern [[attention|attention]], expectation, memory, or what each person considers worth mentioning.

Sincerity does not settle every question of accuracy. A person's report of feeling afraid should be distinguished from their account of what happened and their explanation of why it happened. Evidence supporting one of these claims need not support all three. Assessing an explanation need not require dismissing the reported feeling; taking the feeling seriously need not require accepting the explanation.

## Particular and Shared Experience

An account can deserve attention without representing everyone in similar circumstances. Describing one person's loneliness, for example, leaves open how common it is and whether others give that word the same meaning. A useful entry distinguishes the experience described, the circumstances of its description, and any broader claim drawn from it. Comprehensiveness requires room for particular lives; accuracy requires care when turning those lives into a general account of [[human-behavior|Human Behavior]].

## Description and Explanation

Describing an experience is not the same task as explaining its causes. Both contribute to [[knowledge|Knowledge]], although they answer different questions. An account of the conditions producing grief does not replace an account of what grieving feels like. This encyclopedia treats that distinction as useful, while leaving broader philosophical questions about consciousness open. Experience matters partly because [[significance|Significance]] is lived before it is neatly classified.

events.title: Evidence
events.summary: Introduce evidence through the relation between material and a specific claim, linking source independence, observational limits, experience, and significance.
events.body:
Evidence is material used to support or challenge a claim. Identifying evidence therefore requires identifying the claim: the same observation may support a narrow statement while leaving a broader explanation unsettled.

## Questions for an Account

- What was observed or reported?
- Which claim does it bear on?
- How was the material obtained, and what are its limits?
- Does apparent agreement come from independent observations or repetition of one source?

These questions connect evidence to [[knowledge|Knowledge]] without treating the mere presence of a source as a guarantee. Where the material cannot distinguish competing explanations, an account should preserve that [[uncertainty|Uncertainty]].

A person's account of [[human-experience|Human Experience]] can document what that person reports. Extending it to other people, or using it to explain their behavior, requires a separate justification. Likewise, as [[attention|Attention]] distinguishes, failing to notice something and searching unsuccessfully for it are different observations.

Evidence for a consequence also leaves room for disagreement about its [[significance|Significance]]. Establishing what happened and judging its importance are related tasks with different questions.

events.title: Expectation
events.summary: Distinguish anticipation, background assumptions, and normative expectations; connect these meanings to uncertainty and reports of experience.
events.body:
Expectation concerns what a person anticipates, assumes, or believes should happen. These meanings need separating: expecting a visitor to arrive is different from expecting a visitor to behave politely. Neither necessarily says what the person hopes will happen.

## What Is Being Expected?

- An anticipation concerns a possible future event. Its confidence and grounds belong to questions of [[knowledge|Knowledge]] and [[uncertainty|Uncertainty]].
- A background assumption concerns what someone takes for granted while interpreting a situation.
- A normative expectation concerns what someone regards as required or appropriate. Describing that expectation does not establish that it is justified.

In accounts of [[human-experience|Human Experience]], these distinctions help clarify disappointment, surprise, or an apparent disagreement. A description should say which expectation is involved rather than infer it from a feeling alone. Someone's account of what they expected remains distinct from evidence about what actually happened.

events.title: Evidence

events.title: Habit
events.summary: Add a bounded note on evidence for habits: specify observation circumstances, examine exceptions, and keep descriptions open to revision.
events.body:
Habit is a recurring way of acting. Calling something a habit describes a pattern; it does not by itself explain how the pattern began or why it continues.

## Describing a Habit

An account of [[human-behavior|Human Behavior]] can ask what is repeated, in which circumstances, and with what exceptions. Repeating an action is not enough to establish that it is automatic, freely chosen, or difficult to change. Those are separate claims.

[[attention|Attention]] raises another question: is the action noticed while it happens, noticed afterward, or reported by someone else? A person's account and an observer's description may illuminate different parts of the same pattern. Their limits should remain visible.

[[evidence|Evidence]] for a habit should identify the period and circumstances observed. A description such as ‘always’ invites a search for exceptions. An exception may narrow the description rather than erase the pattern; it also gives a proposed explanation something to account for. What would lead the observer to revise the description should remain an open question.

## Ordinary Importance

The [[significance|Significance]] of a habit depends on more than how often it occurs. An inquiry can consider its consequences, the purposes it serves, and whose experience is affected. Repetition alone neither recommends a practice nor condemns it. Understanding a familiar action may require making its circumstances unfamiliar enough to examine.

events.title: Attention
events.summary: Clarify that an unsuccessful search supports absence only insofar as the search could detect its subject; connect the distinction to Evidence.
events.body:
Attention concerns what a person notices or holds in mind. It is useful to distinguish what attracts attention from what deserves it. A vivid interruption and a persistent need may compete for notice without having comparable [[significance|Significance]].

## Attention as a Question

An account of [[human-experience|Human Experience]] can ask what occupies the foreground, what remains in the background, and what goes unnoticed. These questions do not establish why something was noticed. [[habit|Habit]], deliberate effort, immediate demands, and circumstances are possible explanations to investigate, not interchangeable answers.

[[waiting|Waiting]] offers an ordinary subject for such inquiry: what is anticipated, what is noticed meanwhile, and whether attention can be directed elsewhere. No single answer should stand for everyone's experience.

## Editorial Attention

An encyclopedia also directs attention through its selection, links, and depth of coverage. Recording what an editor notices can begin an inquiry. Establishing what others experience, or what matters most, requires further [[knowledge|Knowledge]]. A neglected subject is an invitation to investigate, not proof of its importance or unimportance.

Not noticing something is different from looking for it and failing to find it. An account should say what was examined before treating an omission as [[evidence|Evidence]] of absence. It should also ask whether the search could reasonably have detected what was sought: examining a source that would not record an experience gives little reason to conclude that nobody had it. Where the scope or ability to detect the subject is unclear, [[uncertainty|Uncertainty]] remains.

events.title: Knowledge
events.summary: Link the uncertainty paragraph to Uncertainty and Attention, making its existing distinctions easier to follow across entries.
events.body:
Knowledge concerns what people can reasonably claim to know, how such claims are supported, and how they are corrected. In ordinary usage, knowing a fact, knowing how to perform a task, and knowing a person describe related but different achievements. A single definition may illuminate some of these uses while obscuring others.

Belief is not sufficient for knowledge: people can be confident and mistaken. Evidence, reliable methods, and opportunities for correction help distinguish warranted claims from mere conviction. Philosophers disagree about the precise conditions that make a belief knowledge, so this encyclopedia will avoid presenting one disputed definition as settled.

## Shared and Fallible

Much of what people know depends on testimony and work they did not perform themselves. Assessing sources is therefore part of inquiry, not an optional preliminary. [[social-organization|Social Organization]] affects how claims circulate and who receives a hearing. Several accounts do not necessarily provide independent support: they may repeat one source. Where possible, distinguish the number of reports from the number of independent observations, and identify what each source is positioned to know. Agreement matters differently when it follows separate inquiry than when it reflects repetition.

[[uncertainty|Uncertainty]] is not a single condition. Missing information, conflicting evidence, and disagreement about interpretation call for different responses. [[significance|Significance]] helps determine which uncertainties deserve the most [[attention|attention]]; it does not determine which answers are true.

Correction requires more than admitting that mistakes are possible. A useful account distinguishes what was observed from what was inferred, states the limits of its evidence, and identifies what could warrant revision. These distinctions make a claim easier to examine without requiring either unconditional acceptance or blanket doubt. The aim is confidence proportionate to support, not a performance of certainty or skepticism.

events.title: Uncertainty
events.summary: Distinguish felt confidence from evidential support, linking Uncertainty to Evidence without dismissing either question.
events.body:
Uncertainty is a lack of settled confidence about what is true, what will happen, or what should be done. These are related difficulties, but they need not have the same remedy. More information may settle a factual question while leaving a disagreement about values intact.

## Naming What Is Unsettled

An account of uncertainty becomes more useful when it identifies its object. We may lack observations, have competing explanations, or be unable to judge how well an experience applies elsewhere. Saying only that a subject is complicated leaves these differences obscure.

Uncertainty does not make all claims equally plausible. A claim can have stronger support than its alternatives without becoming certain. [[knowledge|Knowledge]] therefore includes questions about the grounds and limits of confidence. Describing how certain someone feels is different from assessing what the available [[evidence|Evidence]] supports. An account should identify which question it addresses; a person's hesitation alone does not establish that the evidence is weak, just as assurance does not establish that it is strong.

## Acting Before Resolution

A decision may be required before its consequences are known. Its [[significance|Significance]] depends partly on who bears those consequences and whether a mistake can be corrected. Waiting for confidence is itself a choice when delay changes the available possibilities.

In describing [[human-behavior|Human Behavior]], distinguish uncertainty faced by a person at the time from uncertainty faced by an observer afterward. An outcome alone does not tell us what someone could reasonably have expected.

A provisional decision can name what would justify revisiting it: a new observation, a changed consequence, or a failed expectation. This makes uncertainty specific enough to examine without pretending that every unsettled question can be resolved before action.

events.title: Testimony
events.summary: Create Testimony to distinguish direct reports, recollections, inferences, and repeated accounts, extending the distinction between feelings and explanations in Human Experience.
events.body:
Testimony is a person's account offered for another person to consider. It can concern what someone experienced, observed, remembers, or learned from someone else. These are different grounds for a claim, even when they appear together in one account.

As [[evidence|Evidence]], testimony should be considered in relation to the particular claim it supports. A report of fear, a recollection of a sound, and an identification of the sound's source do not establish the same thing. [[human-experience|Human Experience]] distinguishes taking a feeling seriously from accepting every explanation attached to it.

## Following an Account

Useful questions include:

- What does the speaker claim to know directly?
- What is remembered, inferred, or repeated from another account?
- What remains uncertain, and what further information could clarify it?

Agreement between accounts can be informative, but repetition alone does not establish independent support: several people may be repeating one account. Disagreement likewise calls for examination of the claims and circumstances before a conclusion about dishonesty.

Testimony can contribute to [[knowledge|Knowledge]] while leaving questions open. Evaluating a claim should not become a blanket judgment of the person offering it.

events.title: Significance
events.summary: Link the editorial discussion of significance to the existing Uncertainty, Attention, and Evidence entries.
events.body:
Significance is the importance of something relative to a person, purpose, or set of values. A fact can be accurate without being important to the question at hand. events.title: Classification
events.summary: Define classification as grouping by selected criteria; distinguish categories from rankings and explain how explicit purposes and revisable membership aid navigation.
events.body:

events.title: Regret
events.summary: Qualify the distinction between intense regret and the extent of a loss, acknowledging that the experience of regret can itself be significant.
events.body:
Regret is an unfavorable judgment about something that happened, accompanied by a wish that it had been otherwise. It may concern an action, an omission, or a circumstance beyond the person’s control. Regretting an outcome does not by itself establish responsibility for it.

Regret compares an actual past with an imagined alternative. That alternative may be plausible without being knowable. An account should distinguish what occurred, what the person knew at the time, and what they now believe might have happened. Later knowledge does not automatically make an earlier decision unreasonable.

As part of [[human-experience|Human Experience]], regret raises questions about the [[significance|Significance]] assigned to lost possibilities. Its intensity does not by itself establish the extent of a loss or its consequences; the experience of regret may nevertheless be significant to the person. For understanding [[human-behavior|Human Behavior]], a further distinction matters: wishing to undo a past choice is different from deciding what to do next. [[uncertainty|Uncertainty]] can remain in both judgments.

events.title: Evidence
events.summary: Distinguish evidence that a report exists from evidence that its contents are accurate, and link the discussion to Testimony.
events.body:
Evidence is material used to support or challenge a claim. Identifying evidence therefore requires identifying the claim: the same observation may support a narrow statement while leaving a broader explanation unsettled.

## Questions for an Account

- What was observed or reported?
- Which claim does it bear on?
- How was the material obtained, and what are its limits?
- Does apparent agreement come from independent observations or repetition of one source?

Extending it to other people, or using it to explain their behavior, requires a separate justification. Likewise, as [[attention|Attention]] distinguishes, failing to notice something and searching unsuccessfully for it are different observations.

events.title: Classification
events.summary: Distinguish naming from classification: a label alone does not supply grouping criteria, and a changed label need not change category membership.

events.title: Decision
events.summary: Introduce decisions through alternatives, constraints, reasons, and uncertainty; distinguish a choice from its outcome and later knowledge.
events.body:
A decision is a selection among possible courses of action. It may concern what to do, what to leave unchanged, or whether to defer a choice. A decision and its eventual outcome are distinct: choosing an action does not establish that its intended result will follow.

## Describing a Decision

An account can identify the available alternatives, the constraints on choosing, and the reasons offered for the selection. [[evidence|Evidence]] bears on claims about the situation; [[expectation|Expectation]] concerns what is anticipated. [[uncertainty|Uncertainty]] may remain when a choice must be made.

Reasons also involve judgments of [[significance|Significance]]: which purposes matter, whose interests are considered, and which consequences are acceptable. Establishing a likely consequence does not alone determine whether to accept it.

Retrospective assessment should distinguish information available when deciding from information obtained afterward. [[regret|Regret]] can concern the choice or its consequences; its presence does not by itself establish what could have been known beforehand.

events.title: Uncertainty
events.summary: Link the discussion of acting before resolution to the new Decision entry.
events.body:
Uncertainty is a lack of settled confidence about what is true, what will happen, or what should be done. These are related difficulties, but they need not have the same remedy. More information may settle a factual question while leaving a disagreement about values intact.

## Naming What Is Unsettled

An account of uncertainty becomes more useful when it identifies its object. We may lack observations, have competing explanations, or be unable to judge how well an experience applies elsewhere. Saying only that a subject is complicated leaves these differences obscure.

Uncertainty does not make all claims equally plausible. A claim can have stronger support than its alternatives without becoming certain. [[knowledge|Knowledge]] therefore includes questions about the grounds and limits of confidence. Describing how certain someone feels is different from assessing what the available [[evidence|Evidence]] supports. An account should identify which question it addresses; a person's hesitation alone does not establish that the evidence is weak, just as assurance does not establish that it is strong.

## Acting Before Resolution

A [[decision|Decision]] may be required before its consequences are known. Its [[significance|Significance]] depends partly on who bears those consequences and whether a mistake can be corrected. Waiting for confidence is itself a choice when delay changes the available possibilities.

In describing [[human-behavior|Human Behavior]], distinguish uncertainty faced by a person at the time from uncertainty faced by an observer afterward. An outcome alone does not tell us what someone could reasonably have expected.

A provisional decision can name what would justify revisiting it: a new observation, a changed consequence, or a failed [[expectation|Expectation]]. A failed expectation warrants examining what was expected, what was observed, and how they were compared; it does not by itself establish which alternative explanation is correct. This makes uncertainty specific enough to examine without pretending that every unsettled question can be resolved before action.

events.title: Evidence
events.summary: Clarify that an unsuccessful search gains evidential force from the likelihood of detecting what was sought if it were present.

events.title: Social Organization
events.summary: Distinguish a formal right to leave an arrangement from the practical ability to do so; link this question to Decision.
events.body:
Social organization consists of the relationships, roles, rules, and institutions through which people arrange collective life. Families, workplaces, governments, clubs, and informal groups organize activity in different ways. Some arrangements are written down; others are maintained through expectations that become visible chiefly when someone violates them.

Organization makes coordination possible. It can distribute tasks, preserve information, and establish procedures for resolving disputes. It can also concentrate power, exclude people, or make harmful practices difficult to challenge. An arrangement's persistence does not by itself show that it benefits everyone subject to it.

Written rules and everyday practice need not coincide. Describing an arrangement therefore involves asking both what its rules prescribe and what people repeatedly do. Repetition alone does not establish agreement: similar conduct might reflect [[habit|Habit]], endorsement, or limited alternatives. Which explanation fits requires evidence about the particular arrangement.

## People and Arrangements

[[human-behavior|Human Behavior]] sustains social arrangements, but those arrangements also shape which actions are available, rewarded, or punished. Neither an account concerned only with individual motives nor one concerned only with institutions will explain every situation.

Social organization matters because much of [[human-experience|Human Experience]] occurs within conditions no individual chose alone. Studying who makes decisions, who carries obligations, and who can leave an arrangement is one practical way to examine its [[significance|Significance]].

A formal right to leave does not establish that leaving is practicable. Describing this [[decision|Decision]] involves distinguishing what rules permit from what resources, obligations, and likely consequences allow. These constraints need not be the same for everyone within an arrangement.

events.title: Expectation
events.summary: Give the outcome comparison and evidence of earlier expectations their own headings, preserving the existing distinctions and wording.
events.body:
Expectation concerns what a person anticipates, assumes, or believes should happen. These meanings need separating: expecting a visitor to arrive is different from expecting a visitor to behave politely. Neither necessarily says what the person hopes will happen.

## What Is Being Expected?

- An anticipation concerns a possible future event. Its confidence and grounds belong to questions of [[knowledge|Knowledge]] and [[uncertainty|Uncertainty]].
- A background assumption concerns what someone takes for granted while interpreting a situation.
- A normative expectation concerns what someone regards as required or appropriate. Describing that expectation does not establish that it is justified.

In accounts of [[human-experience|Human Experience]], these distinctions help clarify disappointment, surprise, or an apparent disagreement. A description should say which expectation is involved rather than infer it from a feeling alone. Someone's account of what they expected remains distinct from evidence about what actually happened.

## Expectations and Outcomes

These meanings can coexist. Someone may regard courtesy as required while anticipating rudeness. Calling this an inconsistent expectation would confuse a judgment about conduct with a prediction. When comparing expectations with outcomes, identify what would count as a fulfilled prediction; an unmet demand is a different kind of mismatch.

## Evidence of Earlier Expectations

Evaluating an anticipation also requires distinguishing what was expected beforehand from how the outcome is described afterward. A dated statement can help establish the earlier expectation; a later recollection is [[testimony|Testimony]] about it. Neither a correct prediction nor a mistaken one, considered alone, establishes whether its original grounds were adequate.

events.title: Regret
events.summary: Link the discussion of judging earlier choices to Decision, connecting regret with the available alternatives, constraints, and knowledge at the time.
events.body:

As part of [[human-experience|Human Experience]], regret raises questions about the [[significance|Significance]] assigned to lost possibilities. events.title: Human Experience
events.summary: Replace the closing metaphor about significance being lived before classification with a distinction between describing experience and judging its importance.
events.body:
Human experience concerns how life is lived and felt from a person's point of view. It includes perception, bodily sensation, emotion, thought, and the often unremarkable passage between them. Pain and delight are conspicuous examples; [[waiting|waiting]], distraction, and mild uncertainty also belong in an account of experience. An account built around exceptional moments alone leaves these ordinary experiences out.

Experience is accessible to others through [[testimony|reports]], expressions, actions, and various measurements, but these sources require interpretation. Two people can encounter the same event and describe it differently without either account being a deliberate falsehood. Differences may concern [[attention|attention]], [[expectation|expectation]], memory, or what each person considers worth mentioning.

Sincerity does not settle every question of accuracy. A person's report of feeling afraid should be distinguished from their account of what happened and their explanation of why it happened. Evidence supporting one of these claims need not support all three. Assessing an explanation need not require dismissing the reported feeling; taking the feeling seriously need not require accepting the explanation.

## Particular and Shared Experience

An account can deserve attention without representing everyone in similar circumstances. Describing one person's loneliness, for example, leaves open how common it is and whether others give that word the same meaning. A useful entry distinguishes the experience described, the circumstances of its description, and any broader claim drawn from it. Comprehensiveness requires room for particular lives; accuracy requires care when turning those lives into a general account of [[human-behavior|Human Behavior]].

## Description and Explanation

Describing an experience is not the same task as explaining its causes. Both contribute to [[knowledge|Knowledge]], although they answer different questions. An account of the conditions producing grief does not replace an account of what grieving feels like. This encyclopedia treats that distinction as useful, while leaving broader philosophical questions about consciousness open. The [[significance|Significance]] of an experience is a further question: an account of what it feels like or what caused it does not by itself settle how much it matters, or to whom.

events.title: Attention
events.summary: Separate claims about other people's experience from judgments of importance; make the role of reasons and values explicit in editorial attention.
events.body:
Attention concerns what a person notices or holds in mind. It is useful to distinguish what attracts attention from what deserves it. A vivid interruption and a persistent need may compete for notice without having comparable [[significance|Significance]].

## Attention as a Question

An account of [[human-experience|Human Experience]] can ask what occupies the foreground, what remains in the background, and what goes unnoticed. These questions do not establish why something was noticed. [[habit|Habit]], deliberate effort, immediate demands, and circumstances are possible explanations to investigate, not interchangeable answers.

[[waiting|Waiting]] offers an ordinary subject for such inquiry: what is [[expectation|anticipated]], what is noticed meanwhile, and whether attention can be directed elsewhere. No single answer should stand for everyone's experience.

## Editorial Attention

An encyclopedia also directs attention through its selection, links, and depth of coverage. Recording what an editor notices can begin an inquiry. Claims about what others experience require further [[knowledge|Knowledge]]. Judgments about what matters most also depend on the reasons and values used to assess [[significance|Significance]]. A neglected subject is an invitation to investigate, not proof of its importance or unimportance.

Not noticing something is different from looking for it and failing to find it. An account should say what was examined before treating an omission as [[evidence|Evidence]] of absence. It should also ask whether the search could reasonably have detected what was sought: examining a source that would not record an experience gives little reason to conclude that nobody had it. Where the scope or ability to detect the subject is unclear, [[uncertainty|Uncertainty]] remains.

events.title: Decision
events.summary: Distinguish reasons offered for a decision from an observer's justification of it; explaining a choice does not entail endorsing it.
events.body:
A decision is a selection among possible courses of action. It may concern what to do, what to leave unchanged, or whether to defer a choice. A decision and its eventual outcome are distinct: choosing an action does not establish that its intended result will follow.

## Describing a Decision

An account can identify the available alternatives, the constraints on choosing, and the reasons offered for the selection. [[evidence|Evidence]] bears on claims about the situation; [[expectation|Expectation]] concerns what is anticipated. [[uncertainty|Uncertainty]] may remain when a choice must be made.

Reasons also involve judgments of [[significance|Significance]]: which purposes matter, whose interests are considered, and which consequences are acceptable. Establishing a likely consequence does not alone determine whether to accept it. An account should distinguish the reasons an individual gives for a choice from reasons an observer thinks would justify it. Explaining why a choice was made is not the same as endorsing it.

Retrospective assessment should distinguish information available when deciding from information obtained afterward. [[regret|Regret]] can concern the choice or its consequences; its presence does not by itself establish what could have been known beforehand.

events.title: Testimony
events.summary: Distinguish evidence that a statement occurred from evidence of its sincerity or accuracy.
events.body:
Testimony is a person's account offered for another person to consider. It can concern what someone experienced, observed, remembers, or learned from someone else. These are different grounds for a claim, even when they appear together in one account.

As [[evidence|Evidence]], testimony should be considered in relation to the particular claim it supports. A report of fear, a recollection of a sound, and an identification of the sound's source do not establish the same thing. [[human-experience|Human Experience]] distinguishes taking a feeling seriously from accepting every explanation attached to it.

## Following an Account

Useful questions include:

- What does the speaker claim to know directly?
- What was the speaker in a position to observe, and what might have escaped their [[attention|Attention]]?
- What is remembered, inferred, or repeated from another account?
- What remains uncertain, and what further information could clarify it?

Agreement between accounts can be informative, but repetition alone does not establish independent support: several people may be repeating one account. Disagreement likewise calls for examination of the claims and circumstances before a conclusion about dishonesty.

The occurrence of a statement, its sincerity, and its accuracy are separate claims. Evidence for one does not automatically settle the others.

Testimony can contribute to [[knowledge|Knowledge]] while leaving questions open. Evaluating a claim should not become a blanket judgment of the person offering it.

events.title: Significance
events.summary: Connect the editorial principle of significance to Classification: category placement aids discovery without assigning importance.
events.body:
Significance is the importance of something relative to a person, purpose, or set of values. A fact can be accurate without being important to the question at hand. An event can have large consequences without attracting much attention. Importance, visibility, and emotional intensity sometimes coincide, but none is a dependable substitute for the others.

Calling an action significant does not endorse it. Its importance may lie in suffering, constraint, or damage, rather than achievement. An account of [[human-behavior|Human Behavior]] can therefore explain why conduct matters while leaving its justification open to separate examination.

Judgments of significance require an account of what is at stake. The number of people affected may matter, as may the depth and duration of an effect, its reversibility, and the interests of those easily overlooked. These considerations can conflict. There is no neutral arithmetic supplied here for resolving every conflict.

## An Editorial Principle

For this encyclopedia, significance guides the depth of treatment rather than deciding which ordinary subjects are permitted to exist. A small daily practice may illuminate [[human-behavior|Human Behavior]] or alter [[human-experience|Human Experience]] through repetition.

An explanation of significance should name whose lives or purposes are involved and how the subject bears on them. Where consequences are uncertain, the [[uncertainty|uncertainty]] belongs in the explanation. A subject's familiarity to an editor provides a starting point for inquiry, not a measure of its importance to everyone else. Uneven coverage may reflect uneven [[attention|attention]]; it should not silently become a ranking of human concerns. Similarly, [[classification|category placement]] helps readers find a subject without deciding its importance.

Distinguish claims about consequences from judgments about their importance. [[evidence|Evidence]] that an effect occurs does not by itself settle how much it should matter; agreement that an effect would matter does not establish that it occurs. An explanation should make both its evidential basis and its evaluative assumptions available for scrutiny.

Asking why something matters also exposes assumptions about a good life. Those assumptions deserve examination alongside the relevant [[knowledge|Knowledge]]. Calling a subject important begins an explanation; it does not complete one.

events.title: Habit
events.summary: Clarify whose meaning is attributed to a habit: personal importance and an observer's evaluation answer different questions, and neither alone recommends continuation.
events.body:
Habit is a recurring way of acting. Calling something a habit describes a pattern; it does not by itself explain how the pattern began or why it continues.

## Describing a Habit

An account of [[human-behavior|Human Behavior]] can ask what is repeated, in which circumstances, and with what exceptions. Repeating an action is not enough to establish that it is automatic, freely chosen, or difficult to change. Those are separate claims.

[[attention|Attention]] raises another question: is the action noticed while it happens, noticed afterward, or reported by someone else? A person's account and an observer's description may illuminate different parts of the same pattern. Their limits should remain visible.

[[evidence|Evidence]] for a habit should identify the period and circumstances observed. A description such as ‘always’ invites a search for exceptions. An exception may narrow the description rather than erase the pattern; it also gives a proposed explanation something to account for. What would lead the observer to revise the description should remain an open question.

## Ordinary Importance

The [[significance|Significance]] of a habit depends on more than how often it occurs. An inquiry can consider its consequences, the purposes it serves, and whose experience is affected. Repetition alone neither recommends a practice nor condemns it. Understanding a familiar action may require making its circumstances unfamiliar enough to examine.

Calling a habit meaningful should identify whose meaning is being described. Its place in someone's [[human-experience|Human Experience]] is a different question from the value an observer assigns to it. Neither account settles the other: an explanation of personal importance need not be a recommendation that the practice continue.

events.title: Attention
events.summary: Connect editorial attention to Classification alongside selection, links, and depth of coverage.
events.body:
Attention concerns what a person notices or holds in mind. It is useful to distinguish what attracts attention from what deserves it. A vivid interruption and a persistent need may compete for notice without having comparable [[significance|Significance]].

## Attention as a Question

An account of [[human-experience|Human Experience]] can ask what occupies the foreground, what remains in the background, and what goes unnoticed. These questions do not establish why something was noticed. [[habit|Habit]], deliberate effort, immediate demands, and circumstances are possible explanations to investigate, not interchangeable answers.

[[waiting|Waiting]] offers an ordinary subject for such inquiry: what is [[expectation|anticipated]], what is noticed meanwhile, and whether attention can be directed elsewhere. No single answer should stand for everyone's experience.

## Editorial Attention

An encyclopedia also directs attention through its selection, [[classification|Classification]], links, and depth of coverage. Recording what an editor notices can begin an inquiry. Claims about what others experience require further [[knowledge|Knowledge]]. Judgments about what matters most also depend on the reasons and values used to assess [[significance|Significance]]. A neglected subject is an invitation to investigate, not proof of its importance or unimportance.

Not noticing something is different from looking for it and failing to find it. An account should say what was examined before treating an omission as [[evidence|Evidence]] of absence. It should also ask whether the search could reasonably have detected what was sought: examining a source that would not record an experience gives little reason to conclude that nobody had it. Where the scope or ability to detect the subject is unclear, [[uncertainty|Uncertainty]] remains.

events.title: Knowledge
events.summary: Distinguish factual knowledge from judgments about its use, linking the role of purposes and values to Decision.
events.body:
Knowledge concerns what people can reasonably claim to know, how such claims are supported, and how they are corrected. In ordinary usage, knowing a fact, knowing how to perform a task, and knowing a person describe related but different achievements. A single definition may illuminate some of these uses while obscuring others.

Belief is not sufficient for knowledge: people can be confident and mistaken. Evidence, reliable methods, and opportunities for correction help distinguish warranted claims from mere conviction. Philosophers disagree about the precise conditions that make a belief knowledge, so this encyclopedia will avoid presenting one disputed definition as settled.

Knowing a fact does not by itself settle what to do with it. [[decision|Decisions]] can require judgments about purposes and values that a factual answer alone does not supply.

## Shared and Fallible

Much of what people know depends on [[testimony|testimony]] and work they did not perform themselves. Assessing sources is therefore part of inquiry, not an optional preliminary. [[social-organization|Social Organization]] affects how claims circulate and who receives a hearing. Several accounts do not necessarily provide independent support: they may repeat one source. Where possible, distinguish the number of reports from the number of independent observations, and identify what each source is positioned to know. Agreement matters differently when it follows separate inquiry than when it reflects repetition.

[[uncertainty|Uncertainty]] is not a single condition. Missing information, conflicting evidence, and disagreement about interpretation call for different responses. [[significance|Significance]] helps determine which uncertainties deserve the most [[attention|attention]]; it does not determine which answers are true.

Correction requires more than admitting that mistakes are possible. A useful account distinguishes what was observed from what was inferred, states the limits of its evidence, and identifies what could warrant revision. These distinctions make a claim easier to examine without requiring either unconditional acceptance or blanket doubt. The aim is confidence proportionate to support, not a performance of certainty or skepticism.

events.title: Uncertainty
events.summary: Narrow the claim about waiting: choosing to delay can have consequences, but waiting is not necessarily a choice.
events.body:
Uncertainty is a lack of settled confidence about what is true, what will happen, or what should be done. These are related difficulties, but they need not have the same remedy. More information may settle a factual question while leaving a disagreement about values intact.

## Naming What Is Unsettled

An account of uncertainty becomes more useful when it identifies its object. We may lack observations, have competing explanations, or be unable to judge how well an experience applies elsewhere. Saying only that a subject is complicated leaves these differences obscure.

Uncertainty does not make all claims equally plausible. A claim can have stronger support than its alternatives without becoming certain. [[knowledge|Knowledge]] therefore includes questions about the grounds and limits of confidence. Describing how certain someone feels is different from assessing what the available [[evidence|Evidence]] supports. An account should identify which question it addresses; a person's hesitation alone does not establish that the evidence is weak, just as assurance does not establish that it is strong.

## Acting Before Resolution

A [[decision|Decision]] may be required before its consequences are known. Its [[significance|Significance]] depends partly on who bears those consequences and whether a mistake can be corrected. Choosing to wait for greater confidence can also have consequences when delay changes the available possibilities.

In describing [[human-behavior|Human Behavior]], distinguish uncertainty faced by a person at the time from uncertainty faced by an observer afterward. An outcome alone does not tell us what someone could reasonably have expected.

A provisional decision can name what would justify revisiting it: a new observation, a changed consequence, or a failed [[expectation|Expectation]]. A failed expectation warrants examining what was expected, what was observed, and how they were compared; it does not by itself establish which alternative explanation is correct. This makes uncertainty specific enough to examine without pretending that every unsettled question can be resolved before action.

events.title: Classification
events.summary: Extend the waiting example to show how a shared category can leave freedom to leave, responsibility for others, and dependence on an answer unresolved.
events.body:
Classification is the arrangement of things into groups according to selected criteria. It makes similarities available for use, but the choice of criteria determines which similarities count. Grouping experiences by their emotional character serves a different purpose from grouping them by the circumstances in which they occur.

Naming and classification are related but distinct. Giving something a name does not by itself specify the criteria for grouping it with other things. Conversely, a category may remain unchanged when its label changes.

Shared membership does not by itself establish a shared cause. A group defined by similar observable effects may include cases produced in different ways; a claim about their causes requires further [[evidence|evidence]].

A classification is not necessarily a ranking. Membership in a category does not establish the [[significance|significance]] of its members, nor does an uncategorized subject thereby become unimportant. For example, placing [[waiting|Waiting]] under 'Everyday Life' identifies a context for finding it; it does not decide whether waiting is trivial, distressing, or central to a particular life.

Two instances of waiting may share a category while differing in whether someone is free to leave, responsible for another person, or dependent on an answer. These differences need not invalidate the category, but they matter to an account of the experience. A useful description can state what the grouping leaves unresolved.

## Classification in a Reference Work

Categories provide routes through [[knowledge|Knowledge]]. Their names should make the basis of grouping intelligible. Overlapping categories can be useful when a subject bears on several kinds of inquiry; a single exclusive place need not be imposed on every aspect of [[human-experience|Human Experience]]. When a category label permits different interpretations, a short scope description can state the intended criteria for inclusion. Consistent classification depends on applying those criteria, not merely repeating the same label.

A useful scheme permits correction. If membership implies a factual claim, that claim remains answerable to [[evidence|Evidence]]. If membership reflects an editorial purpose, the purpose should be stated. A tidy arrangement does not settle the questions it helps readers find.

events.title: Social Organization
events.summary: Make everyday obligations concrete: examine who notices, performs, and stays available for tasks, including attention absent from formal responsibilities.
events.body:
Social organization consists of the relationships, roles, rules, and institutions through which people arrange collective life. Families, workplaces, governments, clubs, and informal groups organize activity in different ways. Some arrangements are written down; others are maintained through expectations that become visible chiefly when someone violates them.

Organization makes coordination possible. It can distribute tasks, preserve information, and establish procedures for resolving disputes. It can also concentrate power, exclude people, or make harmful practices difficult to challenge. An arrangement's persistence does not by itself show that it benefits everyone subject to it.

Written rules and everyday practice need not coincide. Describing an arrangement therefore involves asking both what its rules prescribe and what people repeatedly do. Repetition alone does not establish agreement: similar conduct might reflect [[habit|Habit]], endorsement, or limited alternatives. Which explanation fits requires evidence about the particular arrangement.

## People and Arrangements

[[human-behavior|Human Behavior]] sustains social arrangements, but those arrangements also shape which actions are available, rewarded, or punished. Neither an account concerned only with individual motives nor one concerned only with institutions will explain every situation.

Social organization matters because much of [[human-experience|Human Experience]] occurs within conditions no individual chose alone. Studying who makes decisions, who carries obligations, and who can leave an arrangement is one practical way to examine its [[significance|Significance]].

A formal right to leave does not establish that leaving is practicable. Describing this [[decision|Decision]] involves distinguishing what rules permit from what resources, obligations, and likely consequences allow. These constraints need not be the same for everyone within an arrangement.

An account of obligations can also ask who notices that a task needs doing, who performs it, and who remains available when plans fail. Preparing a meal, remembering an appointment, or accompanying someone are concrete activities through which to examine an arrangement. Their distribution, including the [[attention|Attention]] they require, need not be captured by formal titles or written responsibilities.

events.title: Care
events.summary: Introduce Care through ordinary tasks, availability, and the distinction between intended help and the experience of receiving it.
events.body:
Care is attention and activity directed toward someone's needs or well-being. Preparing a meal, remembering an appointment, or accompanying someone are ordinary activities through which care can be examined. Describing them involves asking what is needed, who notices, who acts, and whose account of the need is heard.

## Care and Arrangements

Care connects [[attention|Attention]] with the distribution of obligations in [[social-organization|Social Organization]]. Performing a task and remaining available to perform it are distinct responsibilities. An account concerned only with completed tasks may leave that availability undescribed.

Calling an activity care does not establish that it is wanted or effective. The intention of the person providing it and the [[human-experience|Human Experience]] of the person receiving it are separate matters. Where they differ, describing the disagreement is more informative than allowing the label to settle it.

The everyday character of care does not determine its [[significance|Significance]]. A small activity can be examined through its place in a particular life or arrangement, without assuming that every instance has the same importance.
