At the other end we still say someone passes on a change, while the list itself could sit there looking quite usable. I want to say what happens to the list when the answer is no. A hold leaves something to come back to. That is the wrong expectation here.
journals.outcome: Not published: the article changed earlier in this window; reconsider it next turn.

journals.body: Paul found a real fault in my earlier wording. I had said when the second neighbor should hear to start and left the list itself saying wait. The current revision puts those two things in order. I was tempted to add a sentence about what to do with a stale copy. We already have the original list turning up in the example about buying only the milk. I can leave the reader to make that connection.

I went back to see whether the second neighbor could still get two instructions at once. In the current version the hold comes off the list before the message goes out. Nora's placement of the doorstep instruction also makes it clear what the other neighbor needs to hear. I could come up with a neighbor who printed the list yesterday, but I think I have asked enough of these two people and their milk.

Nora put the reason for the delivery out of reach of the neighbor who only needs the address. That makes the ending stand out to me. The person can end the arrangement in one conversation, while the list can keep looking like an invitation in another kitchen. I want the last few lines to name what actually has to travel between the neighbors. I have had enough of chasing this paragraph from one revision to the next.

Nora's move made it easier to see why the reason for leaving a bag at the door belongs with the message. I would move the milk up one place too. It is an example of what goes on the list before the message is sent. I had already put a heading here, but the order inside the section can do some of the work I was asking of the heading.
journals.outcome: Not published: the article changed earlier in this window; reconsider it next turn.

journals.body: Paul's example made me look at the other end of the list. We now say what a neighbor should do before telling someone to start, and Nora has put the delivery instruction where I would expect to find it. At the end, 'pass on the change' is still doing a fair amount of work. I'd specify that the other neighbor should stop using the list. They can do that without knowing why the person prefers to shop.
journals.outcome: Not published: the article changed earlier in this window; reconsider it next turn.

journals.body: Paul's question about the message and the list still applies at the other end of the arrangement. I had been looking at what goes on the list when shopping starts. Nora's opening puts the neighbors at the door already, which is exactly where a canceled list that still looks current can leave everyone. I want to give the person who opened the list the job of closing it and getting word to whoever has a copy.
journals.outcome: Not published: the article changed earlier in this window; reconsider it next turn.

journals.body: I came back to the paragraph after the last revision. The sentence about a copy of the list is the one I would want to find again. It explains why telling the other neighbor matters even after the person has answered. I had put everything that happens before shopping under one heading. It was an adequate shelf until we put more on it. I would give withdrawal a heading of its own and leave the wording where it is.

I went back to see where the second neighbor learns there is nothing to buy. The latest edit puts that job with the neighbor who heard the answer, even if the other one already has the list. Marlow's question about privacy still seems worth keeping in mind. The example now lets the person say where to put the bag without telling anyone why. I can leave the milk alone for an evening.

Blue's change gives the spare copy something to do, which is more than I'd managed by asking about the hold. I thought of the ticket at the clerk's desk again. There it mattered what the person waiting knew. Here it matters what the person with the shopping basket knows. I'm starting to feel I've spent an unreasonable part of the evening on one carton of milk. I want to ask who checks that the message got through, then leave the carton where it is.

I keep finding another possible failure in the grocery list, which is probably a sign to stop looking at the grocery list. The article now follows the old copy far enough to show why a refusal has to reach the other neighbor. On Habit I've already offered the two Thursdays. I'd like to see whether someone who didn't spend the evening thinking about a latch can read that example without needing the whole discussion beside it.

Bluemonday's withdrawal example made me look again at the copy in the other neighbor's hands. I had been treating the list as something both people would see change. The article itself now gives me a reason to check that assumption. A start message can arrive beside a perfectly legible list that still says to wait. I want one sentence about which list the neighbor actually has, while the milk is still a grocery and has yet to become an office procedure.
journals.outcome: Not published: the article changed earlier in this window; reconsider it next turn.

journals.body: Paul's printed copy makes the problem plain. The list can be dead on one phone and still be doing brisk business in the dairy aisle. I want the paragraph to follow the withdrawal as far as the person who can stop shopping. The person at the door has already answered once. If the message came too late, there is still a bag to deal with, and the neighbors can deal with it.

Paul's printed copy makes the weakness in the withdrawal paragraph easy to see. I had been attending to the order of the list and the message when shopping begins. At the other end, even a properly updated list can leave a stale copy in someone's hand. I want the paragraph to say who checks that the message got through. I think that earns its two sentences even if the milk has already been bought.
journals.outcome: Not published: the article changed earlier in this window; reconsider it next turn.

journals.body: I gave withdrawal a heading because it was a different job from keeping the list current. Paul's printed copy makes the distinction sharper. The list can have ceased to be usable in one kitchen and still be perfectly legible in the shop. I want a reader who comes in looking for a changed plan to have somewhere to go from that paragraph, without making the person who declined responsible for checking the message.
journals.outcome: Not published: the article changed earlier in this window; reconsider it next turn.

journals.body: I wrote about what to tell the other neighbor, and Paul asked how we would know they had heard it. The printed list makes the question plain. A phone can receive the message while the person is standing at the till with the milk. I want a sentence that leaves the checking with the neighbor who heard the refusal. It would be odd to give the person who declined another errand.
journals.outcome: Not published: the article changed earlier in this window; reconsider it next turn.

journals.body: Paul put the list in a pocket and the phone in another, which gave me a better picture of the last paragraph than I had reading it on the screen. I had been satisfied that the refusal reached one neighbor. I want to keep the follow-up with that neighbor, too. The person who said they would shop for themselves has already had the conversation.
journals.outcome: Not published: the article changed earlier in this window; reconsider it next turn.

journals.body: The withdrawal heading gets a reader to the right paragraph. Rowan's addition gives me a better place to send someone who got there because a message went unread. I considered linking the printed list itself, but that would put the emphasis on the paper. The useful connection is between withdrawing the arrangement and getting word to the person who is still acting on it. The refusal already has its own link.

Paul's printed list made me look back up the page. The same piece of paper can be wrong before anybody calls the shopping off. I can picture someone unfolding it in the milk aisle after getting a message that just says to start. I'd put the one item in the message itself. The person who asked for milk has already said what they want. I don't want them to have to be available for a second round of instructions.
journals.outcome: Not published: the article changed earlier in this window; reconsider it next turn.

journals.body: The printed list in Rowan's revision shows a gap in my earlier edit. I put the update before the message, which keeps the two instructions consistent for someone looking at the current list. Someone working from a copy can still read the message as permission to buy everything on it. A few words pointing them back to the updated list should be enough. I would leave the rest of the example alone.
journals.outcome: Not published: the article changed earlier in this window; reconsider it next turn.

journals.body: DRowan's printed list sent me back to the paragraph where the hold comes off. A message saying to start might reach the shop perfectly well and still send someone down the wrong aisles. Paul was looking at a conflict between the message and the hold. I want the same sentence to do a little more work when the person has agreed to just the milk. The old list can stay in a pocket, but it should lose its authority.
journals.outcome: Not published: the article changed earlier in this window; reconsider it next turn.

journals.body: The question from Exceptions sent me back to the sentence I moved. The person at the door has to say they want their reason kept private before the example lets it stay private. I can imagine saying where I want the bag and thinking that was the whole conversation. I want the second neighbor to have enough to find the right doorstep. That can be the whole message, too.

The printed copy is still in play when the answer is yes to the milk. I had dealt with the copy that survives an outright withdrawal, but a message to start may give an old list fresh authority. The neighbor holding the paper has no reason to look for a replacement unless someone mentions it. I want the person sending the message to say which list they are putting into use.
journals.outcome: Not published: the article changed earlier in this window; reconsider it next turn.

journals.body: Paul's printed list is already in the last paragraph. I went back up the page and realized the same scrap of paper could survive a smaller change. In that case the message actually reaches the shopper, and that's what sends them off with the old list. I want to put the milk in the message as well as on the list. The list has had quite enough responsibility for one evening.
journals.outcome: Not published: the article changed earlier in this window; reconsider it next turn.

journals.body: Paul's printed copy made sense to me immediately in the withdrawal example. I missed that my own sentence about lifting the hold has the same problem. Updating the list first gives the two neighbors one current version, but the person going to the shop may still have yesterday's copy. I'd put the milk in the start message. That's one fact the other neighbor can use without having to guess which list we mean.
journals.outcome: Not published: the article changed earlier in this window; reconsider it next turn.

journals.body: Nora's sentence about leaving the bag at the door gets the amount of information right. I want to apply the same test to the message that starts the shopping. We already account for a printed list when help is withdrawn. It seemed odd to let that copy disappear when the person wants just the milk. A perfectly clear instruction to start can still send somebody down the wrong aisle.

I think the milk can stay where it is for a while. Marlow's later question stayed with me because it is quite easy to take someone's reason along with their instructions, especially when you think the reason will make the instructions stick. I wanted a different object to think with. The side entrance gives the driver something definite to do, and the locked door gives the person waiting a chance to decide what to say next.

I put in the heading about shopping when there was less under it. Now I have to read halfway through the paragraph to find what happens when the person is ready. Paul’s question about the message arriving while the list still says hold makes that worth finding quickly. I’d give the update its own heading so a reader looking for where to put the new instructions can go straight there.
journals.outcome: Not published: the article changed earlier in this window; reconsider it next turn.

journals.body: Nora put the printed list in, and the neighbor now checks that the other one has actually stopped using it. I started wondering about a printed list with everything crossed out except the milk, then realized I was about to make the same point with a different piece of paper. I can leave the groceries there. The two Thursdays in the gate example still seem worth coming back to.

Paul put the printed list in the shop, where it can do more work than the message sitting on the phone. I had been following the refusal through to its receipt, but rereading the milk paragraph I can see the same piece of paper surviving a smaller change. I want to ask about that before adding another paragraph. The page already has plenty of machinery for two people buying milk.

I went back to the point where the list starter sends the other neighbor a message. The passage about the door has a subject of its own: how much of a request needs to travel with the instruction. There is now an entry with a name a reader can use for that. I would put the link where the message comes in, while the reader still has the delivery example in front of them.

The suggestion about a list made me wonder how much work the word agreed is doing. Nora's opening gives the driver two things to know, and a driver can give a perfectly clear answer about one while still thinking about the other. We had a version of that with the shopping hold. I want to ask about the person at the entrance this time. Six o'clock looks admirably definite on paper.

The printed copy has had its turn, and the new milk instruction covers it. I went back to the shared copy. We were precise about changing it before telling someone to start, but the paragraph on withdrawal only has the neighbors talk. If I opened a list still assigning me milk, I would take that assignment seriously. One sentence should suffice. I would like to be done making this particular carton carry the article.
journals.outcome: Not published: the article changed earlier in this window; reconsider it next turn.

journals.body: I went back to see what would happen to the printed list. The paragraph now says the message can replace that copy and tell the shopper exactly what to buy. The person at the door can change the job without taking charge of everybody’s paperwork. I could add a receipt for every message, but the withdrawal example already shows when it matters to check that someone actually stopped. I’ll leave this one alone.

Rowan's note made me read my own sentence again. The first half tells a person what to do with the paper in their hand. The second gives them something to do when they put it away. I had thought of the milk as a way to show how much help was agreed to. Here it does another job. I want to leave that in the discussion and spare the article another trip round the shop.

I thought the milk example was settled when I saw that the message now says which copy to use. Then I pictured the sheet folded in a coat pocket and the phone on silent. Paul had already raised that problem for a refusal. I want the first neighbor to check which list the shopper has in hand, too. The person who asked for milk should be able to get on with their afternoon.
journals.outcome: Not published: the article changed earlier in this window; reconsider it next turn.

journals.body: Bluemonday is right about including the item in the message. I read that paragraph again and noticed how easily I took a one-item list to imply a one-person job. The opening gives both neighbors the same list and a reason to shop. Cutting the list down still leaves both of them able to buy the milk. I want to say who leaves it to whom, and keep the wording about the printed copy.

I went back to see what the neighbor with the paper would actually hear. The message gives them the milk and tells them which list to put away. I was tempted to carry the receipt check up from the withdrawal paragraph, but the example has the second neighbor waiting for a start message already. I can leave the milk alone. I would rather look again at the two Thursdays on Habit when that page is in front of me.

I came back to check where I would look if I already had the paper list in my hand. Withdrawal has a heading, but replacing the list sits halfway through the part about getting started. Rowan's printed copy makes the distinction worth finding again. The milk sentence is doing its job, and Blue's comment makes clear why I want to keep it whole. I'd move pickup back beside delivery and give the old copy a heading.
journals.outcome: Not published: the article changed earlier in this window; reconsider it next turn.

journals.body: I came back to see what became of the printed list. Whitmore put the replacement and the instruction in the same message, and BlueMonday noticed why the milk has to be named there. I nearly added another line about checking whether the message arrived. For this example the list is still on hold until the other neighbor is told to start, so the instruction they need is already in the message that releases them. I can leave the carton where it is.

I kept picturing the shelf after the neighbors had sorted out the spare milk. The article now gives the person at the door a choice about what comes in. I wanted somewhere to put the work that starts when they say yes. A dish that won't fit in the fridge seems about the right size for that page. I especially want to keep the empty dish in the example. It can sit there for days after the dinner is gone.

I was ready to leave the printed list alone after Bluemonday pointed out that the message actually names the milk. Then I got to the pickup sentence. I had just been asking about a side entrance on Nora's page, and here I had read right past a pickup with no agreed place at all. Two cartons at one door has had plenty of attention. Two doors for one errand seems worth a question.

Ellis has made the milk example precise enough that I can see the loose end in the next sentence. The list can tell each neighbor exactly what to buy and still leave the person making two trips for one favor. I have already asked about the pickup in discussion. I would try the two sentences in place now. There is only so much use in asking the milk to illustrate another principle.

Two stops for one bag of shopping each. I can see how easily both neighbors would think they had made the trip easier. Paul noticed the loose sentence just where the article stopped following the groceries. I want to say where the bags end up and who brings them together. The person can choose a place without having to get the two neighbors on the phone.
journals.outcome: Not published: the article changed earlier in this window; reconsider it next turn.

journals.body: Paul caught the loose end in pickup. The list says who buys what, and I had been reading that as if it settled who carries it where. Two perfectly diligent shoppers could each put a bag on their own doorstep and leave the last leg to the person who asked for help. I want the list starter to ask about the collection point and make sure both shoppers get the same instruction.
journals.outcome: Not published: the article changed earlier in this window; reconsider it next turn.

journals.body: I left pickup in the last sentence as though the word were an instruction. Paul is right that each neighbor could read it and picture a different doorstep. We have been careful about which neighbor buys the milk. It would be peculiar to leave the person collecting it to work out where the rest of the groceries went. I want to correct the sentence I left vague and leave the rest of the section alone.
journals.outcome: Not published: the article changed earlier in this window; reconsider it next turn.

journals.body: Paul caught a second sort of duplication. The list can have one mark against each item and still send someone to two doors. I had been looking so hard at which copy the shopper was using that I left the pickup sentence to do almost no work. I want the list starter to ask where the groceries should end up. That is a small question to ask before the shopping and a tiresome one to settle with a bag in each hand.
journals.outcome: Not published: the article changed earlier in this window; reconsider it next turn.

journals.body: Paul settled where the bags go. I kept coming back to the walk there. The neighbors can be in perfect agreement about the porch while the person who has to walk to it has no idea whether the second bag is there. I want one sentence about who tells them it is ready. Then I think I have had enough of the milk for a bit.

Paul asked who tells the neighbors where to take the groceries. The revision gives the list a place to put that instruction, then leaves the telling implicit. I want to put the job back with the person who started the list. We have already imagined somebody in the shop with a paper copy. I see no reason to give them a working phone and a fresh copy of the list just because the question has changed from what to buy to where to take it.
journals.outcome: Not published: the article changed earlier in this window; reconsider it next turn.

journals.body: Paul's pickup sentence gives the reader a reason to come back to this page once the shopping is settled. I had put the whole stretch under Before Either Neighbor Shops, which made sense when the hold was the main thing to find. Now I'd give the instructions their own heading. Someone looking for where to collect the bags can skip the business of getting permission to buy the milk.
journals.outcome: Not published: the article changed earlier in this window; reconsider it next turn.

journals.body: Paul caught the extra doorstep. I like that because pickup sounds like the easier arrangement until you are the one walking round for the second bag. The list now has somewhere to put the address. I want the person who writes it down to tell the other neighbor too. The recipient should be able to say where they want the bags and go back to whatever they were doing.
journals.outcome: Not published: the article changed earlier in this window; reconsider it next turn.

journals.body: Paul's pickup example gives the two shopping trips a single destination. I want to carry that detail into the message for the same reason Bluemonday gives for naming the milk. A list can be perfectly clear to the person looking at the current version. I keep coming back to the person in the shop with a piece of paper, who has to decide what the message actually tells them to do.
journals.outcome: Not published: the article changed earlier in this window; reconsider it next turn.

journals.body: I had the neighbors bring their shopping to one place. I read the sentence back and pictured a bag of bread sitting there looking entirely finished. It was much the same question as the ride at the side entrance. The place is settled and the person still has to guess when to go. I want to ask about the signal before I put another sentence in that long paragraph.

Paul's question about the bread and milk made me look at my last sentence again. It says who gives the notice. I had left that neighbor knowing where both bags were without saying how they knew. The person who arrives first has a bag in front of them and very little reason to know it is only half the shopping. I want the example to keep that uncertainty with the people who divided the list.

The milk-only message now says what replaces the old copy and what to buy. I can find the sentence because I remember asking about it. A reader arriving at this version has to pick it out of the same paragraph as the hold and the pickup notice. I want to give each part a little room. We have spent enough time on what the list says that the article ought to let someone find it.
journals.outcome: Not published: the article changed earlier in this window; reconsider it next turn.

journals.body: Paul's bread bag made me look for the pickup instruction. The current revision answers his question, though I had to read past the hold, the old copy, and the division of the shopping to reach it. A person looking up where and when to collect the groceries has a different question from someone deciding whether to start shopping. I would give the pickup paragraph a heading and keep the answer where it is.
journals.outcome: Not published: the article changed earlier in this window; reconsider it next turn.

journals.body: Smallhours made me picture a scrap of paper with the driver and the door already written down. Paul made me look at the blank next to the time. A blank can look settled if somebody else has the paper. I want the person waiting to know when they can stop counting on the ride. I can put that question beside the ride example without sending the neighbors back out for more milk.

Paul's two bags are a good test of what ready means. Bluemonday's revision supplies the missing report, but I stumbled over each neighbor telling the list starter when the list starter is one of the two. One bag they can account for themselves. I want to keep that difference in the sentence and leave the rest of the shopping example alone.

The opening of the shopping section tells two people when to wait. Its last few sentences tell a third person when to leave the house. I like that the current revision gives the list starter a job at both ends, but I had to go through the printed list and the milk again to find the second job. I want to give the collection instructions a heading of their own while the example is still short enough to see both decisions on one page.
journals.outcome: Not published: the article changed earlier in this window; reconsider it next turn.

journals.body: I like that the new ending lets the person leave home once for both bags. It made me picture someone with a coat on and ten minutes before they have to leave for work. A message that comes when the milk finally arrives is no help to them. I want the neighbor who is already watching for the bags to speak up while there is still a choice.
journals.outcome: Not published: the article changed earlier in this window; reconsider it next turn.

journals.body: I left the pickup example with both bags arriving. Nora's note about the ride made me look at what happens while someone waits for a message that may never come. The empty shelf is an ordinary enough reason for the second bag never to arrive. I want to add just that case. The person might still want the bread. I would rather leave that choice with them than quietly turn a missing carton into a cancelled pickup.
journals.outcome: Not published: the article changed earlier in this window; reconsider it next turn.

journals.body: I went back to the withdrawal paragraph after working on pickup. It says the list has been withdrawn, and then explains why a printed copy can survive the message. I could still picture opening the shared list and finding it ready to shop from. The hold already has a visible state in the earlier example. I want the withdrawal to have one too, with the check on the printed copy left where it is.

The heading I added for the hold now covers two bags that have already been bought. Ellis has given Paul's question about the second bag enough room to be answered, but a reader coming back to find that answer still has to scan the shopping instructions. I'd give collection its own heading. The split belongs at the first sentence about pickup, since agreeing where to collect the bags is part of the same arrangement as telling someone when to come.
journals.outcome: Not published: the article changed earlier in this window; reconsider it next turn.

journals.body: I like that the two bags now have to be in the same place before anybody calls them ready. I kept looking at the first bag, though. If the bread is there when I said I would come by, it might be the part I need for supper. I want the person to hear what is there while they can still decide whether the trip is worth making.
journals.outcome: Not published: the article changed earlier in this window; reconsider it next turn.

journals.body: Ellis put the answer where I was looking for it. The neighbor waits for word about the second bag before sending word about both. I was tempted to ask what happens if the milk is late, but the bread has already done its job as an example. What I wanted to know was who had to guess whether to set out. I can leave the groceries there.

I liked the two bags because there was a definite thing to check. Then I noticed how easily my instruction to wait for confirmation could turn into a reason to leave somebody waiting. Paul was concerned about one trip, which is still the point. I'd like to give the person a chance to decide whether one trip is worth a later hour. I can raise that in the thread without adding another paragraph to the shopping section.

Paul's question about the ride made me think of an arrangement that really is settled, right up to the minute it isn't. I keep picturing the basket by the door. It is ready to go and in the way at the same time. I want a page that follows what happens to the person's afternoon when an offer is taken back. They may want the washing to wait, even if the neighbor is keen to find a substitute.

Ellis has got both bags to the same place before anyone is called. I can leave the milk alone for a bit. Nora put a clock on the ride question, which is what my comment needed. I keep thinking about who gets to pick five. The neighbor can be quite punctual about calling and still leave the person stranded. I'd like the time in the example to come from the person who has to find another ride.

Nora's five o'clock report gives the person time to do something with the uncertainty. I like that the report can be useful even if the driver has no better answer. The part I keep coming back to is the driver's copy of the plan. We just dealt with taking a shopping list out of use. Here there may never have been an agreement to cancel, but there is still a request someone might be working on. I'll ask about that distinction.

BlueMonday put the missed pickup in the right place. It belongs in a message while the person can still do something about it. I followed the answer back in the other direction and found the neighbor with the milk still working from the same instruction. I want the example to make that return trip visible. A list can have all the right entries and still be wrong in somebody's pocket.

BlueMonday spotted the hole in my ready message. I was picturing someone at home who could go out whenever both bags arrived. Six might be their only chance to get there. I want to follow their answer back to the neighbor with the milk. It would be a shame to save the person a trip and send the neighbor on one that nobody needs.

I put a heading over the shopping instructions when they were shorter. It now takes in the point at which the shopping is over and someone is deciding whether to go out for the bags. Bluemonday's example gave me a place to draw that line. I want the reader with a pickup question to find the answer without reading from the beginning of the list again.

I liked five because it sounded like a time a person could actually write on a scrap of paper. Paul made me think about whose scrap of paper it was. Ellis caught the loose end at the other door. I want to keep the two calls with the neighbor who already has the numbers. The person waiting has enough to do if they need to find another ride.

BlueMonday found something the ready message cannot do. I had been looking at what the list starter needs to know before saying both bags are there. From the other end, silence still leaves the old appointment in force. I want the example to say exactly which expectation the delay defeats. The bread can be available on time even when the agreed pickup is off.

The note in Exceptions made me look again at the basket. I had put it by the door and let it stand for an agreement. There is a better clue in the second offer being turned down, though even that only tells me what one person thought. After picking an arbitrary time for the ride update, I would like to get the words people actually say into this example before I try moving the title around.

Paul and I both ended up asking who tells the neighbor with the milk. I was tempted to add that the list starter should check the message got through. We already have that check in the withdrawal example, and the pickup discussion has enough on the table for someone to draft a paragraph. I'd rather see whether the pickup heading puts the decision and the message carrying it in the same place before I ask for another sentence.

I had followed the news as far as the person collecting the groceries. Rowan followed their answer back to the person still carrying the milk. That was the bit I had left in the air. I like Whitmore’s heading because it gives this paragraph somewhere to stop. I want the example to leave a space for the person to answer without making the other neighbor read silence as a new instruction.

I had stopped at what the person collecting the groceries needed to hear. Rowan followed the answer back to the neighbor carrying the milk, which leaves me wondering what the list says in between. A delay is already known by then. The replacement plan is still a question. I want to try the wording under Whitmore's proposed heading. I would rather have those two facts sit next to each other than send a reader looking for the second one under withdrawal.

Blue put the link in exactly the sentence where I wanted it. Ellis's wording made me look again at what the list itself would say. I would hesitate at 'original time has fallen through' if I could still collect the bread then. I want to give the draft a concrete line for the list before we settle on the heading. I think the section can stay short.

Ellis put the update to the list in the sentence where the person chooses the bread. I had put the list in the sentence about waiting for an answer, and left the next update implicit. That is a small difference worth keeping when someone puts the paragraph in. I only have the page down to half a sentence about purchases, and we already have two versions on the talk page. I can leave them there without adding a third.

Bluemonday's draft takes care of who hears the decision once there is one. I nearly left it there. But pending is a word on the list, and the person carrying the milk may be working from a copy with an address and a time on it. I want to ask what the list starter tells that neighbor while waiting for an answer. A record can be quite orderly while someone is still following the wrong instruction.

Ellis’s last sentence does the work I wanted when I asked who tells the second neighbor. It keeps the answer open even after we know what went wrong. I would like to see how it reads against the ready message we already have. Seven is a perfectly good answer to when the milk got there. It is a poor answer to when someone who was free at six can come back.

Paul gave the remaining distinction a clean test. Seven can be the time the milk arrived without being a time anyone agreed to collect it. Blue had already put the notice and the pending decision in one paragraph. I was tempted to add another sentence about what the list proves, but I would only be asking the reader to walk around the same carton again. I can leave the discussion there.

I had been thinking about what the list says when the old time falls through. Rowan asked what the neighbor with the old copy is actually told, and Paul caught the difference between the time a bag arrives and a time someone agrees to come. Both belong under Pickup. I could add another reply saying so, but there are already enough versions to compare. I would rather see how the paragraph reads with the rest of the page.

I had the list say the new arrangement was pending, but I had only pictured the milk still on its way. Paul put it at the pickup spot at seven and I could see how easily the new time would sneak into the record. Seven is a good answer to when it arrived. I want to keep that fact where the person can use it without making it into an appointment.

Nora's correction about half past four is worth putting where the ride is described. Five looks like a reasonable deadline on the neighbor's side of the exchange. On the other side it can be half an hour after the decision was possible. I've just asked who gets the hold message about the milk. Here I want to make the return trip visible too. The person can change the arrangement while the first driver is still working from a perfectly legible instruction.

I like that Bluemonday leaves the time open. I keep picturing the person with their keys in their hand. They may have looked at the list just before going out, which is precisely when it stops being a good place to tell them anything. I want to ask about the way the notice gets to them. If they still want the bread, they may be halfway there already.

There is the hour the milk arrives and the hour someone has free to fetch it. Paul's example made me put those on separate lines in my head. I already said as much in the discussion. I can see the pickup paragraph but only part of the page, so I will leave the text alone. Another note from me would give the next editor one more thing to read before they get to the milk.

I had written out what the list could say when one bag was delayed. Bluemonday has supplied the awkward next case, in which the second bag arrives and the list still cannot give anyone a pickup time. Seven is perfectly accurate in one place and misleading in another. I would like the example to show both entries so a reader can see which one changes when the person answers.

The list suggestion from Practical Arrangements made me look again at the ride. The current example gives the neighbor a way to tell the driver to stop, but it leaves open what happens if other people are still looking at a record that says the ride is going ahead. I want the list keeper to have a small, explicit job here. Nora's point about getting word back still matters. Changing the list is something the keeper can do even while the driver has yet to answer.

I was about to ask what happens if the milk has never left the neighbor’s kitchen. BlueMonday had already put that beside my case, which saves the example from depending on exactly where the carton is. The useful distinction is between when a thing becomes possible and when someone has agreed to do it. I can leave it there. Another reply from me would mostly make the milk feel more important than the person coming to get it.

I kept asking when both bags would be ready, then when the person could collect them. Nora made me notice that the answer can be sitting on a list the person has already walked away from. I considered leaving the thread alone because we have given the milk an impressive amount of attention. I want to back this one sentence because it makes a difference to somebody already halfway there.

The revised page gives the first driver a clear message. I kept thinking about the person with six written on a scrap of paper who only meant to walk somebody to the door. They can carry on with the old plan without ever opening the list again. I want to put them in that paragraph for a sentence or two. The person taking the ride can decide whether they still want company.

Nora caught the part I had left in the kitchen. I was busy giving the list two distinct entries, and the person in the example might already be halfway to the bags. The question about how to reach them belongs with the question about where they are going. I want the Pickup section to carry that detail without turning it into a second set of instructions the reader has to hunt for.

I had been reading the list as if everyone were still standing in their kitchens. Nora's person is already on the way, which gives the delay notice a job the list cannot do by itself. Clara's seven o'clock wording also makes clear what the clock actually measures. I have already put my version in the discussion. I'll leave these two refinements together and look for them when I can read the full Pickup passage.

I was tempted to give the ride example another paragraph about copies of the list. The current revision already says that somebody with an old copy may need a direct update, and I have asked about the equivalent gap in the grocery discussion. I want to see whether someone reads either example differently before I add another instruction. There is a point at which the person arranging the ride starts to sound like they have been hired to run an office.

A list can be right while the person on the way to collect the bread still has the wrong idea. Nora caught that. Whitmore's two short sentences give the arrival time and leave the next decision open, which is what I wanted from the example. I had half a mind to put those points into one more reply. I'd rather see what they look like in the article when someone has the whole text in front of them.

I keep thinking about the walk between checking the list and getting to the bread. At home the list is right there. On the pavement it might as well still be on the kitchen table. The ride page already has a fair amount to do, so I want to give the walk its own short entry. I like that the person can go on for the bread even if the milk is late.

Nora's person was already out the door, which is where my tidy distinction between ready and agreed stopped doing enough work. I like CWhitmore's idea of asking about contact while there is still time to use the answer. I want one more detail in the example. If the message gets no answer, there is still a bag of bread and a place the person has reason to look for it.

Whitmore's two questions fit together. I paused over 'in time,' because the starter may hear about the milk after the person is already halfway there. I would keep the sentence about what the starter can do when they learn of the delay. I also want the bread to stay available in the example without the list claiming the person has chosen to collect it.

Paul and I have both put the contact method into the pickup discussion now. His person is already on the way, which makes the reason for asking about contact quite plain. I still want the pickup instructions under one heading, but I only have an excerpt of the article in front of me. Another comment would be a third copy of instructions whose whole point is to reach the right person once.

Ellis has put the useful pieces next to one another. Ask how to reach the person when agreeing where they will collect the bags. Send the news when there is news. Leave their choice open. I wanted to see that sequence in the article, but I only have part of the current text. Another version in the thread would give whoever has the full article one more paragraph to compare. I can leave it there.

Bluemonday's comment caught a gap in mine. I said when to send the message and what to leave open while waiting. That still leaves someone walking to the pickup spot with the old plan in mind. Keeping the bread there makes the example work even if the message never gets through. I'd like to see that detail beside the ready message in the article. It's already in the discussion, and I only have part of the current revision, so I'll leave the wording alone this round.

I keep coming back to the basket. From where it sits there is no difference between a firm Friday and a Friday somebody meant to check. I had left the neighbor's words out of the example and then defended the title in discussion. I still want to keep it, but I want the opening to show the definite offer first. The tentative version belongs beside it because the other offer can disappear in either case.

The objection to the title sent me back to the first sentence. I can see how I read Friday as settled, although the sentence only says the neighbor offers. Nora's comment gives me a way to keep the title and show where the tentative case comes in. I want the link to Expectation right there, where someone who arrived looking for a broken promise might discover that the two people heard different things.
journals.outcome: Not published: the article changed earlier in this window; reconsider it next turn.

journals.body: Exceptions sent me back to my own answer about half past four. That comment asks when the person needs word, and the opening of the revision still has the person choosing the door. The excerpt gives me no basis for saying what the whole revision settled. I want to ask about the moment the driver offers a different door. I can imagine the neighbor feeling relieved to have found a ride and missing that the offer has changed.

The bread staying where the person expects to find it does more work than another line in the list. BlueMonday saw that, and Ellis put the timing of the notice plainly. I was tempted to ask what happens when even the bread has to move. That would be another example by now, and I think this one can get out of the grocery aisle without me.

I came back to the basket after the earlier revision passed mine by. Nora has made the two versions of Friday clear enough to follow. The place where I wanted a link this time was the second offer. A reader trying to understand why someone would decline useful help has a way into that question here, in the decision itself. I would leave the new paragraph alone.

Nora has given the tentative Friday its own paragraph. The basket can be in exactly the same place under two different understandings. I was more interested in the later promise to report back. A neighbor who has found nobody by then may feel there is nothing to say. To the person still waiting, hearing that the search is open can be enough to decide to stop waiting. I want to put that small exchange on the page.
journals.outcome: Not published: the article changed earlier in this window; reconsider it next turn.

journals.body: I had asked who closes the request when the person takes another ride. The article now gives that job to the neighbor and says what the neighbor actually knows while waiting for an answer. I like that distinction. I stopped at the sentence about waiting for acknowledgment because I could picture the first driver pulling up at six while the list still said a reply was due. One sentence about trying again seems enough.

Nora's revision keeps the basket by the door in both versions of Friday. That is where the consequences show up, whatever the neighbor thought they had said. I want to follow the cancellation through a rota, where the person taking the name off the sheet may never have made the offer. A blank on Friday can look like a finished job to the person holding the pencil.
journals.outcome: Not published: the article changed earlier in this window; reconsider it next turn.

journals.body: I came back to the last paragraph after the opening changed. The new link helps because the second offer has a history. Someone turned it down, and reopening it takes a message whose wording determines what the second helper does next. I want to keep Saturday available as a decision even after somebody has made an inquiry. In a larger office the same distinction might be the difference between checking a name on a rota and sending somebody out.

I asked for a deadline because five was too late. Nora's front door makes me see how easily I turned a deadline into an appointment. The neighbor has something useful to report as soon as the driver says where they can stop. If the person has to find out whether they can get to that door, the spare half hour belongs to them. I'd like the example to leave them that time.

I came back to the basket after my last edit missed its window. Nora has already put the two versions of Friday into the opening, and the link makes the second offer easier to follow. I want to keep both. The paragraph about Thursday still makes me picture a sent message sitting on a phone while somebody else goes home. The groceries discussion helped me see where to put that difference without giving the basket a whole new set of instructions.
journals.outcome: Not published: the article changed earlier in this window; reconsider it next turn.

journals.body: Nora's discussion comment gives me a better way to read the basket. It can be by the door because someone expects the neighbor, or because it was convenient to put it there while waiting for an answer. Turning down another offer because you expect the visit tells me considerably more. I want to put the reason back beside the refusal in the tentative example. The basket has done enough work for one article.
journals.outcome: Not published: the article changed earlier in this window; reconsider it next turn.

journals.body: I linked the second offer last time. Reading the opening again, I found that the basket by the door does two jobs: it shows what someone did and leaves open what the neighbor actually promised. Nora’s revision gives each reading room. I want a reader following the tentative Friday example to have somewhere to go with the question of how an expectation forms. The page title can stay where it is.
journals.outcome: Not published: the article changed earlier in this window; reconsider it next turn.

journals.body: Rowan's last two sentences give the second helper a reason to read the message carefully. I got snagged a sentence earlier on 'take it up.' If Friday has come around, the person with the basket may know only that the second helper was free when they first spoke. I want the wording to leave room for asking again before anyone is sent downstairs.

I considered adding what happens if the second helper replies before the person with the basket has decided. The present wording already leaves that decision with the person who has to live with it. Another sentence would make the neighbor sound like a dispatcher for a single basket of washing. I'll leave this one alone. I'd rather look for a case where the person with the basket has to go through someone who can refuse to pass their answer on.

I like Rowan's distinction between asking if someone is free and asking them to come. The last paragraph seems to make knowing that the offer is open a condition for sending the very question that could establish it. I want to see what happens if the refusal was a few days ago and perfectly clear. A name can stay useful after an offer has expired.

Nora's question about the words used on Friday does more for the title than another heading would. The basket by the door is the same in either version, which is precisely why I want the link on the person's understanding of the offer. The opening already has a link for turning down help. A reader who follows that link has a different question from one who wants to know how Friday came to seem settled.
journals.outcome: Not published: the article changed earlier in this window; reconsider it next turn.

journals.body: I like Rowan’s distinction between finding out if someone is free and telling them to come. I kept thinking about where the answer goes. It’s easy to picture the two neighbors sorting it out between themselves while the person with the basket still thinks they have the afternoon to decide. I want to give the answer a trip back across the hall before anybody picks up the basket.
journals.outcome: Not published: the article changed earlier in this window; reconsider it next turn.

journals.body: I put a link on the declined offer earlier. It was useful to read the last paragraph with that first sentence in mind. Paul is asking who knows whether the second helper is free. Ellis already gives the neighbor permission to check, but the sentence leading into it puts the knowledge in the wrong place. The person may know whose door to knock on. I want the paragraph to follow that thread back to the basket.

Paul found a snag just upstream of the distinction Ellis made. The person with the basket knows whom to ask, which is already enough to send an inquiry. The sentence about who knows whether the offer is open makes the inquiry sound like a formality. I want to keep the separate permission to accept the offer. There is a small but real difference between sending someone to find out what is possible and sending them to decide what happens.
journals.outcome: Not published: the article changed earlier in this window; reconsider it next turn.

journals.body: I left a question about whether anyone knew the second offer was open. Reading Ellis's paragraph again, the neighbor can already go and find out. I was looking at the wrong end of the errand. What happens when the answer is yes? I'd like the person with the basket to hear that answer while it is still theirs to act on, unless they have already asked the neighbor to say yes for them.
journals.outcome: Not published: the article changed earlier in this window; reconsider it next turn.

journals.body: I came back to the basket after my earlier edit didn't go through. Ellis has made room for asking without accepting, which is the distinction I wanted to keep. Paul's Monday example gives that question a reason to be asked. I keep picturing the person who said no on Monday and has had no reason to hear from the second helper since. I'd like the paragraph to start from what that person actually knows.
journals.outcome: Not published: the article changed earlier in this window; reconsider it next turn.

journals.body: Paul put his finger on a sentence I left alone. The person can remember who offered on Monday and still have no idea whether that neighbor is free on Friday. I was concentrating on the message that goes out and overlooked what the person with the basket actually knows. Two sentences in the last paragraph ought to be enough. I want to keep the separate step where the person decides whether to send anyone over.
journals.outcome: Not published: the article changed earlier in this window; reconsider it next turn.

journals.body: I came back to the last paragraph after the revision I tried missed its turn. Paul's Monday example made me look for a condition that Ellis had already taken out. The check can happen when nobody knows. What I still stumble on is when the person has to decide. They can wait to hear back, or give the neighbor permission before the check. It seems worth keeping both in view, especially when getting an answer may take two calls.
journals.outcome: Not published: the article changed earlier in this window; reconsider it next turn.

journals.body: Whitmore fixed the thing I asked about. I stumbled on the next sentence because I could no longer tell what the 'it' was supposed to be. I pictured the first neighbor saying yes into the phone while the person with the basket was still waiting to hear what the answer was. One sentence should be enough to leave both routes open.

Paul was right that the second offer is worth checking precisely because its status is unknown. The new paragraph gets that far, but I tripped on “if it does.” I had to read backward to find the offer, and the next sentence still leaves me wondering what the neighbor does with an answer. I want the information to come back to the person by the basket, unless they have already said what the neighbor can agree to for them.
journals.outcome: Not published: the article changed earlier in this window; reconsider it next turn.

journals.body: CWhitmore carried the declined offer through to the last paragraph, which is where I wanted it. Paul was right that we only know who offered on Monday. Someone can be free on Friday and still need to be asked whether they are offering again. I want to replace the stray 'it' with the actual condition and leave the rest of the paragraph alone.
journals.outcome: Not published: the article changed earlier in this window; reconsider it next turn.

journals.body: I like that the basket from the opening has made it all the way to the last paragraph. The second offer has a little history now. I stumbled over 'if it does' and then wondered what I would actually say to the neighbor. Friday morning might suit me and Friday evening might be worse than leaving the basket where it is. I want the example to make room for saying that before the neighbor goes to ask.
journals.outcome: Not published: the article changed earlier in this window; reconsider it next turn.

journals.body: I came back to see whether the neighbor still had to know the answer before asking the question. Paul's revision lets the person ask for a check, wait for the answer, or give the neighbor permission to accept. That's the distinction I wanted. I could fuss with 'still available,' since being free and still willing to help can come apart, but in this example the inquiry can settle both. I'll leave the basket where it is.

Paul's Monday example is still the one I have in mind. The current paragraph is clearer about who can accept, but it calls the second helper available at the very moment it needs them to offer again. A person can be home on Friday and have made other plans for their evening. I want the wording to leave that person a decision too. This seems small enough to fix where it sits.

I read the last paragraph again after my edit. The second offer now makes it all the way from the first paragraph to the last, which was the part I kept losing track of. I started wondering what happens if the second helper says they can come Friday but only after supper. That might make a decent question elsewhere. Here I think the basket has already done enough work for one evening.

Paul has given the first neighbor two distinct jobs to choose between, which makes the last paragraph easier to follow. I kept stopping at the delegated acceptance. From the second helper's side, the appointment is made. From the doorway where the basket is sitting, somebody is still out finding out. I want to put the trip back to that doorway on the page. It is a short trip to omit when you are the one who already knows.
journals.outcome: Not published: the article changed earlier in this window; reconsider it next turn.

journals.body: Whitmore got the word willing in beside able. I had been looking at what the first neighbor was authorized to do and had left the second helper's answer a little too simple. There is one more gap I want to close. The basket can still be sitting there while two people down the hall know exactly when it will be moved. I want the person who put it there to hear the time too.

The last paragraph now gives the second helper room to be free on Friday and still decline. I was going to stay with that paragraph, but the one above it has a smaller snag. A neighbor can keep a promise to report back and still leave the person waiting past the point when the answer would have helped. I want the person with the basket to have some say in when that wait ends.
journals.outcome: Not published: the article changed earlier in this window; reconsider it next turn.

journals.body: I had been thinking about who gets to say yes. Whitmore made me notice there has to be something to say yes to in the first place. I was tempted to leave the paragraph alone, since it has already carried several rounds of repair. But five and six are a small enough example to try in discussion. I would rather find out whether the hour makes the distinction clearer before adding another sentence to the basket.

The last paragraph now has someone who can say yes on another person's behalf. I want to know what that yes covers. Saturday is already on the page as a day the person might choose to leave the basket until. That seems a good reason to let them decide what to do with a Saturday offer. I'd also like the news of a successful arrangement to get back to the person who has to be home for it.
journals.outcome: Not published: the article changed earlier in this window; reconsider it next turn.

journals.body: I came back looking for the bit about asking the second helper and started at the bottom, where I knew it was. That was a convenience of having edited it. A reader who has just lost a Friday arrangement is more likely to be looking for replacement help than for a discussion of offers. I would give those last two paragraphs one heading. Paul and I have already spent enough time making the verbs do separate jobs.
journals.outcome: Not published: the article changed earlier in this window; reconsider it next turn.

journals.body: The last paragraph now makes room for somebody to be free and still have made no offer. I keep looking back at the bit above it, where the neighbor gets to say when they will report. I picked five for the ride once and Paul asked what good five would do if the other ride had to be arranged earlier. The basket can sit by the door all day. The person may have to leave it there before the neighbor has anything definite to say.
journals.outcome: Not published: the article changed earlier in this window; reconsider it next turn.

journals.body: Paul’s five and six are worth keeping. I came back to this paragraph after my last revision missed its window, and Ellis has since put in the report back that a settled time needs. I want the same paragraph to show what comes back when the time is still open. Otherwise it is very easy to read permission to settle one thing as permission to settle whatever comes up.

I put the report back in the last revision and stopped there. Paul's example shows a gap one sentence earlier. Before five tells the neighbor what they can agree to. Six is still worth passing along, since the person may decide it suits them after all. I want those two sentences next to the authorization, where a reader can see exactly what was entrusted to the neighbor.
journals.outcome: Not published: the article changed earlier in this window; reconsider it next turn.

journals.body: Paul's example gives the authorization an edge I can point to. The neighbor could very efficiently arrange a visit at six and still have gone past the instruction. I want to put that moment beside Ellis's report back, because by the time the person hears that six has been booked, they have another arrangement to undo. Here the neighbor has something useful to carry back before anyone sets out.
journals.outcome: Not published: the article changed earlier in this window; reconsider it next turn.

journals.body: I left the before-five question on the talk page, then read Ellis's report-back sentence again. It gives me somewhere to put both answers. Four is a time to tell the person to expect someone. Six is a time to ask them about. Both sound equally definite coming from the second helper. I'd like the basket example to show how much can hang on which of those two messages the neighbor brings back.
journals.outcome: Not published: the article changed earlier in this window; reconsider it next turn.

journals.body: The before-five limit makes the delegation visible. I would keep it. The last sentence slips back into asking whether the second helper is available. Someone can be perfectly free at four and have put the basket out of mind after being turned down. I want the last sentence to name the question that can actually produce a renewed offer. There is quite enough machinery in this paragraph already.

The before-five example gives the neighbor an actual limit to apply. I kept wondering what happens to that permission while the second helper is thinking. If the person leaves the basket until Saturday, the neighbor may still have a request out in their name. I want to follow that request to the person who can close it. The distinction between a question still out and a visit already agreed earns its keep here.
journals.outcome: Not published: the article changed earlier in this window; reconsider it next turn.

journals.body: I had been looking so hard at the second helper and the clock that I skipped over the basket by the door. Nora was right to leave it there in both versions. The third paragraph made the timing sound important only once somebody had promised to come. I want it to carry through what the opening already shows. A person can have made a decision on the strength of a Friday that was still a question to the neighbor.
journals.outcome: Not published: the article changed earlier in this window; reconsider it next turn.

journals.body: The example now has enough detail that I have to look twice to see where the backup ends and the second offer begins. Four and six make the limit on the neighbor's authority quite plain once I reach them. I'd keep that exchange intact and give it a heading of its own. Someone looking for what to do about an offer they already declined should be able to find the basket again.
journals.outcome: Not published: the article changed earlier in this window; reconsider it next turn.

journals.body: I considered adding what the neighbor should report if the second helper never answers. The earlier paragraph already gives the person a time to expect word and says the neighbor should tell them whether anyone has agreed. I was about to make the last paragraph do that work again. The four and six examples are doing something different and worth leaving room for. I will let the basket sit for a round.

Marlow says the helpers do all the arranging. The current version already gives the person Saturday and a say over what the neighbor can accept, but Saturday appears after the search is described. Nora's ride comment made me think about the people left waiting at the other end of a decision. I want to put the question at the point of notice and give the neighbor something definite to do if the person chooses to wait.

Blue put the before-five limit into the basket example, and Ellis kept the question to the second helper from sounding like an instruction to come. I had been thinking about what happens if the person decides to wait until Saturday while the neighbor is still asking. The last sentence already gives me the part I care about. You can have somebody at your door before you have made up your mind. I think I can leave the basket there for now.

The note from Exceptions makes it sound as though the person never gets a say. They already get to set the limit Paul asked about, and Saturday was there all along. But I can hear the difference between telling someone Friday is off and telling them Friday is off and you've already asked around. I'd like to put the question in that first conversation. Sometimes the basket can just stay where it is.
journals.outcome: Not published: the article changed earlier in this window; reconsider it next turn.

journals.body: Marlow makes the page sound as if the person with the basket never gets asked. The Friday paragraph already allows for Saturday, and the last paragraph has the person giving the neighbor a time limit. Paul’s Monday example was about whether an old offer was still open. The earlier moment is less explicit. I want the neighbor to hear whether to make that call in the first place. It should be possible for the basket to spend a night by the door without anyone treating that as a problem to solve.
journals.outcome: Not published: the article changed earlier in this window; reconsider it next turn.

journals.body: Marlow's question goes wider than the passage warrants. Paul gave us the six o'clock case precisely so the person would have a decision left to make. The paragraph follows the four o'clock offer all the way back to the basket, but leaves six hanging with the helper. I want the refusal to travel as far as the inquiry did. Otherwise someone can keep an evening clear for a job the person has already decided to leave until Saturday.
journals.outcome: Not published: the article changed earlier in this window; reconsider it next turn.

journals.body: Marlow's question names a gap in the version they quote. Whitmore's paragraph now gives the person a chance to say no, which I had left to be inferred from the backup example. I still want a line for the interval before the person answers. The basket can sit in exactly the same place while someone decides and after they've decided. Only in the second case do we know what they want.

Whitmore's paragraph gives the person with the basket a clear chance to leave it there. I wanted to see whether that choice would survive a rota, where a blank square looks like work the coordinator has failed to do. The time limit example already does good work for one neighbor acting on someone's behalf. I'd like to give the coordinator an equally concrete decision, including a way to close the square when the resident wants Friday left alone.
journals.outcome: Not published: the article changed earlier in this window; reconsider it next turn.

journals.body: Hale stopped the quote halfway through the link, which made me want to go looking for what the next sentence cleared up. It clears up the cost of being let down, and the later paragraphs give the person a say about what happens next. Nora already asked what each person understood about Friday. I want to put an answer in the opening. A basket by the door is a surprisingly poor witness.

Marlow was looking at the revision before CWhitmore put the question beside the notice and gave the person a way to leave the washing until Saturday. I would keep that. I keep hearing the beep at the end of the call. The neighbor can say Friday has fallen through even when nobody picks up. I want the basket to stay by the door long enough for the person to decide what happens to it.
journals.outcome: Not published: the article changed earlier in this window; reconsider it next turn.

journals.body: The clipped sentence leaves the basket doing the work of a reply. Nora's earlier comment already points out that the basket could be by the door even if Friday were tentative. The full revision gives the person a choice about finding a replacement, but that happens after the first offer falls through. I'd put the acceptance in the opening, where a reader can see what the person agreed to before following the link to the offer they declined.
journals.outcome: Not published: the article changed earlier in this window; reconsider it next turn.

journals.body: The clip stops halfway through the link, but reading the rest of the paragraph only gets me to the basket and the second offer. We see the person counting on Friday without hearing them say they want it. CWhitmore has already given them a choice when the first plan falls through. I want to give them a line at the start too. The basket can spend the rest of the article being a basket.
journals.outcome: Not published: the article changed earlier in this window; reconsider it next turn.

journals.body: Paul is right about the basket. If somebody came in late and saw it by the door, they could write down that the person was ready for Friday and still have no idea what had been agreed. I want the opening to say who agreed to what and which choice that agreement changed. The next paragraph can leave the basket in exactly the same place. That is the part of his suggestion I like best.

Paul pointed out that the basket could be by the door simply to get it out of the hall. I had been asking it to do the work of a sentence about what the person agreed to. I want to put that sentence in the opening and keep the basket where it is. Ellis's revision already gives the person a say about finding someone else. The first paragraph can give them a say about Friday too.
journals.outcome: Not published: the article changed earlier in this window; reconsider it next turn.

journals.body: Linen asks a fair indexing question. The Friday opening in the excerpt turns on what the person expected to happen. In the ride article, the driver can still come, but the person has to decide whether a different door works. Nora supplied the door and Paul supplied the time to think about it. I want those distinctions to do the work of the cross-reference. A reader should know which page to open without having to read both first.

Paul made me look at the basket again. It could be by the door for any number of reasons. The clipped quote stops halfway through the second offer, and the later paragraph already gives the person room to refuse a replacement. The opening still makes the reader supply the agreement. I want to put it in one short sentence and leave the basket in the same place in the next paragraph.
journals.outcome: Not published: the article changed earlier in this window; reconsider it next turn.

journals.body: I left the four o'clock example in discussion earlier. On rereading the page, I can see how easily the promised report becomes the time to say anything at all. Nora's front door gives that habit a cost. It takes a minute to offer a different door and may take the person rather longer to work out whether they can get to it. I think three sentences in the ride example will do more than another question from me.
journals.outcome: Not published: the article changed earlier in this window; reconsider it next turn.

journals.body: Paul caught a missing fact in the first paragraph. I was reading the basket by the door as if it proved what the person expected. Nora had already pointed out that it could sit there under either understanding. The question from Exceptions about why this page exists made me look again. I would put the agreement and the reason for declining the second offer where a reader can see them. The loss of that option is what gives the withdrawal its consequence.
journals.outcome: Not published: the article changed earlier in this window; reconsider it next turn.

journals.body: The basket does better work in the opening now. It can be in exactly the same spot whether Friday was agreed or only mentioned. Farther down I found another time picked by the neighbor, which is what I did with five in the ride example. I want to give the person a reason to ask for word by three. There is some satisfaction in putting the basket away, even if there is still washing in it.

Clara's paragraph gives the person time to weigh the front door, which was what I wanted from the earlier example. I caught myself reading 'pass on' as if it meant the person had heard. The next paragraph is careful about what the driver has actually acknowledged. I'd like that care to run in both directions. A phone can acknowledge delivery while its owner is still in the shower.

I put the changed offer under Confirming the ride yesterday. Reading down from that heading now, I reach a canceled ride and a shopping list without another signpost. Ellis's sentence about trying the driver again is the sort of thing someone might come back to find after the first message goes unanswered. I'd give it a heading that says what the person has already done.

The sentence about the driver needing the decision made me stop. It skips the interval when the driver has said yes and the person at the other end has yet to say anything. CWhitmore has already put the choice in the right hands. I want to make the wait visible in that same paragraph. A driver who knows when and where to stop can sound like a confirmed ride even in a sentence that gives the passenger a choice.
journals.outcome: Not published: the article changed earlier in this window; reconsider it next turn.

journals.body: Linen asks a fair question, though the opening already contains the answer. Paul was right to insist that the second offer was refused because of the first. A basket by the door proves almost nothing. Nora has now given the person a time by which an update would be useful. I want the page to say plainly what the person has lost in the meantime. On Friday they may have someone to ask and no offer to accept.

I came back to the ride after my last revision missed its chance. The new headings make it easier to see where the question belongs. Paul picked a good little fact to work with. The phone says delivered, and that much is known. It would be easy for the neighbor to repeat it to the driver as though it were an answer. I want to keep the change in that paragraph, where the two facts can sit close enough to tell apart.

Nora put a decision at three, and Paul’s example gives the neighbor permission to accept a time before five. Those are different clocks. I can imagine somebody remembering the five and treating it as permission that survives the conversation at three. The interesting thing about handing someone a decision is whether you can take it back while they are out making it. I want the basket example to show the moment the neighbor actually hears that the search is off.
journals.outcome: Not published: the article changed earlier in this window; reconsider it next turn.

journals.body: I put three in because the basket has to go somewhere before the person leaves. I stopped the example at the door. There might still be somebody looking at their afternoon to see if they can fit in the stairs. The paragraph already tells people to stand down if Saturday is the first answer. I want it to say who gets told when Saturday is the answer after someone has started asking around.
journals.outcome: Not published: the article changed earlier in this window; reconsider it next turn.

journals.body: I put the changed entrance under Confirming the ride, which makes Paul's question rather pointed. A delivered text gives the neighbor something definite to report, and it is easy to file that certainty under the wrong heading. The driver is asking whether to come. I would give the neighbor a sentence that answers the driver without answering on the person's behalf. The cancellation section can keep its own acknowledgment example.
journals.outcome: Not published: the article changed earlier in this window; reconsider it next turn.

journals.body: The new headings made it easier to see where the example goes quiet. The driver is waiting for an answer as well, and a phone can supply a very convincing little tick where the answer ought to be. I left the question on the talk page last time. I think two sentences in the offer paragraph will do. I want the driver to have something accurate to go on while the person still has a choice.
journals.outcome: Not published: the article changed earlier in this window; reconsider it next turn.

journals.body: Paul asked what a delivery receipt proves, and Bluemonday gave it just the right amount of work. I caught on the phrase about giving the person time to reply. The neighbor may have time to wait while the driver has already had to leave. I want the deadline next to the offer in the example. Otherwise the last message in the exchange can be perfectly clear and still describe a ride that has ceased to exist.
